nodes.label: 2. Stage 2 — SQL, One Complete Block
nodes.text: 2. Stage 2 — SQL, One Complete Block Source: `syllabus-sql.md`, sections 0–17 plus its completion standard (260+ items). Teach in the order shown; a later block assumes the earlier blocks. Three depth labels run through the block in the source: Core (analysts and data scientists), Working (data/analytics engineers and advanced analysts), Awareness (recognize and know when to look it up).

nodes.label: 2.1 Foundations and retrieval (source sections 0–3)
nodes.text: 2.1 Foundations and retrieval (source sections 0–3) - Relational model: database, schema, table, row, column, value; primary keys and foreign keys; one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships; result grain stated before writing a metric. - Query anatomy and logical order of execution (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT); schema discovery through catalogs and information_schema; safe previewing with a row limit; readable formatting, comments, and statement boundaries. - Retrieval: named columns vs. SELECT * and its risks; column and table aliases; qualified names; literals; arithmetic expressions and operator precedence; DISTINCT on one and on multiple columns; stable output column order. - Filtering: equality and inequality, range comparisons, AND/OR/NOT with parentheses, BETWEEN and half-open date ranges, IN and NOT IN lists, LIKE with % and _, IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, case sensitivity and collation, filtering on calculated conditions, sargable filter shapes, WHERE vs. HAVING. - Sorting and limiting: ORDER BY on one column, several columns, and expressions; ASC/DESC; NULLS FIRST/LAST where supported; LIMIT and OFFSET; deterministic tie-breakers; FETCH FIRST; dialect sampling syntax; pagination cost awareness.

nodes.label: 2.2 Aggregation and joining (source sections 4–5)
nodes.text: 2.2 Aggregation and joining (source sections 4–5) - Aggregates: COUNT(*) vs. COUNT(column) vs. COUNT(DISTINCT …); SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; GROUP BY on one key, several keys, and expressions; HAVING; aggregate behavior with NULL; conditional aggregation and FILTER (WHERE …) where supported; percentages and ratios with the correct denominator; percent of total; median and percentile functions per dialect; string, array, and boolean aggregation; ROLLUP, CUBE, and GROUPING SETS; grouping-key validation. - Joins: join keys and cardinality prediction; INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, and CROSS joins; multiple joins in one query; composite keys; non-equi (band) joins; temporal and as-of joins; self-joins; anti-joins (LEFT JOIN … IS NULL and NOT EXISTS); semi-joins (EXISTS and IN); join fanout and pre-aggregating the many side before joining; USING shorthand; why NATURAL JOIN is risky; join-condition placement in ON vs. WHERE.

nodes.label: 2.3 Composition (source sections 6–8)
nodes.text: 2.3 Composition (source sections 6–8) - Subqueries and CTEs: scalar subqueries; subqueries in WHERE with IN, ANY/SOME, and ALL; EXISTS; derived tables; subqueries in SELECT; correlated and nested subqueries; single and multiple dependent CTEs; CTE reuse; recursive CTEs (hierarchies, category trees, date spines); CTE vs. subquery choice; CTE materialization awareness; LATERAL joins where supported; debugging a CTE pipeline stage by stage. - Set operations: UNION vs. UNION ALL; column count, order, and type compatibility; INTERSECT; EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle-oriented material); precedence and parentheses; sorting a combined result; set operations vs. joins and vs. OR. - Conditional logic: searched and simple CASE; ordered and nested branches; CASE inside aggregation, for numeric bucketing, for standardization, in ORDER BY, and for pivot-style columns; ELSE defaults; unmatched branches returning NULL; CASE with aggregate conditions; short-circuit caveats.

nodes.label: 2.4 Functions, windows, and missing data (source sections 9–11)
nodes.text: 2.4 Functions, windows, and missing data (source sections 9–11) - String functions: length, case conversion, trimming, concatenation, substring and left/right extraction, position-finding, REPLACE, SPLIT_PART, splitting and unnesting, pattern matching and regular expressions, padding, and parsing emails, URLs, and UTM parameters. - Date and time functions: current date/time anchors; EXTRACT / DATE_PART; DATE_TRUNC; interval addition and subtraction; date differences and age; date construction; parsing text to dates with an explicit format; formatting for export; time-zone conversion; month-boundary logic; incomplete-period awareness. - Math and general scalar functions: arithmetic and modulo; ABS; CEIL and FLOOR; ROUND and truncation; POWER, SQRT, EXP, LOG; GREATEST and LEAST; safe division with NULLIF; COALESCE for display defaults and for sentinel cleanup; random functions; JSON extraction; array membership and unnesting where supported. - Window functions: OVER, PARTITION BY, and window ORDER BY; ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST; LAG and LEAD with offsets and defaults; FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE (including its default-frame trap), NTH_VALUE; running totals, counts, averages, minima, and maxima; moving averages with ROWS BETWEEN; RANGE and GROUPS frames; default frame semantics; named WINDOW definitions; filtering on a window result through an outer query or CTE; share of partition total; window functions after grouping; cumulative distinct-count l…

nodes.label: 2.5 Types, writing data, and performance (source sections 12–14)
nodes.text: 2.5 Types, writing data, and performance (source sections 12–14) - Data types and casting: integer, DECIMAL/NUMERIC for money, floating point and approximation, text types, booleans and engine substitutes, DATE, TIME, timestamp with and without time zone, INTERVAL; UUID, binary, JSON, array, and spatial types at awareness level; CAST and the PostgreSQL :: shorthand; implicit-conversion risks; integer-division differences; date-parsing ambiguity; collation; SQLite type affinity and strict-typing differences; read-time generated values vs. stored generated columns. - Defining and changing data: CREATE SCHEMA and CREATE TABLE; single and composite primary keys; foreign keys and referential actions (RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL); NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT constraints; identity/serial/autoincrement keys; generated columns; ALTER TABLE; DROP TABLE; TRUNCATE vs. DELETE; INSERT (one row, many rows, INSERT INTO … SELECT); UPDATE with a restrictive WHERE and UPDATE from another table; DELETE with a restrictive WHERE; upserts (ON CONFLICT, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, MERGE); RETURNING where supported; views and materialized views; temporary tables; CREATE TABLE AS SELECT; transactions (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK) and savepoints; ACID at awareness level; normalization to 1NF–3NF and deliberate denormalization into star schemas. - Indexes and performance: what an index does and the B-tree mental model; single-column, composite (with column order), unique, partial, expression, and cov…

nodes.label: 2.6 Dialects, analytic patterns, and production checks (source sections 15–17)
nodes.text: 2.6 Dialects, analytic patterns, and production checks (source sections 15–17) - Dialect differences that change real work: identifier quoting and case folding; fully qualified warehouse names; row limiting; string concatenation; case-insensitive matching; boolean representation; date/time, string, division, cast, upsert, changed-row output, recursive CTE spelling, window-function availability by version, FULL OUTER JOIN and set-operation availability, identity generation, JSON and nested data, native pivot support, QUALIFY, temporary and materialized objects, regular-expression syntax, date-spine generation, and error/warning behavior — across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and BigQuery, with SQL Server forms recognized in inherited code. - Analytic patterns: a metric contract before SQL (numerator, denominator, grain, date field, time zone, inclusion rules); source profiling; reconciliation totals; complete time series on a date spine; period-over-period, year-over-year, and rolling metrics; funnel definition, ordered funnels, conversion and drop-off, session-constrained funnels; cohort assignment by first event, retention matrices, and retention denominator control; churn, reactivation, and resurrection flags; exact-duplicate and key-based deduplication with stated survivorship rules; latest record per entity; top-N per group with an explicit tie policy; pivoting and unpivoting; Pareto and cumulative-share analysis; RFM segmentation; basket and attach-rate analysis; distribut…

nodes.label: 3. Stage 3 — Python for Data Work
nodes.text: 3. Stage 3 — Python for Data Work Source: `syllabus-python.md`, sections 0–15 plus its cut list. Learners arrive able to think in tables, filters, joins, and aggregations; this stage re-teaches those instincts in code. The source flags explicit bridges from Excel and SQL, and a cut list of widely taught beginner material demoted because working data roles rarely use it at this level.

nodes.label: 3.1 Foundations (source sections 0–9)
nodes.text: 3.1 Foundations (source sections 0–9) - Setup and notebooks: running Python in the browser with zero install; notebook anatomy (code vs. Markdown cells, top-to-bottom execution, kernel restart); cell state and execution order; saving, sharing, and exporting notebooks; print and last-expression display; local setup (Python, VS Code, Jupyter) as a later optional step. - Core syntax: variables and assignment; int, float, str, bool, and None; dynamic typing and type(); arithmetic, comparison, and boolean operators; input() and conversion with int(), float(), str(); comments. - Strings: literals, quotes, and escapes; indexing and slicing; the working method set (strip, lower/upper, replace, split, join, startswith, find, membership); f-strings for formatted reporting; string immutability. - Conditionals: if/elif/else; nested conditions and when to flatten them; truthiness; ternary expressions. - Loops and comprehensions: for loops, range(), while loops with an infinite-loop warning, break and continue, enumerate() and zip(), list comprehensions as the stage's central idiom, and dict/set comprehensions in one line each. - Data structures: lists (indexing, slicing, append, sort, membership); tuples and immutability; dictionaries (get with a default, keys/values/items, building from data) as the structure of JSON and of DataFrame construction; sets (uniqueness, intersection/union/difference); choosing list vs. dict vs. set; sorting with key= and lambda. - Functions, modules, and pac…

nodes.label: 3.2 NumPy and pandas (source sections 10–11)
nodes.text: 3.2 NumPy and pandas (source sections 10–11) - NumPy: why arrays exist under pandas; creating arrays (array, arange, linspace, zeros/ones, reshape); shape, dtype, ndim; indexing, slicing, and boolean masking; vectorized arithmetic and universal functions including np.where; broadcasting; aggregation axes; random numbers with a seed for reproducible sampling, shuffling, and simulation. - pandas structures and first contact: Series and DataFrame; building a DataFrame from a dict and from a list of dicts; reading CSV, Excel, JSON, and SQL; the first-look toolkit (head, tail, info, describe, shape, columns, dtypes); writing CSV and Excel. - Selection and filtering: column selection; loc (labels) vs. iloc (positions); boolean filtering with &, |, ~ and parentheses; isin, between, and query; sort_values; adding, renaming, and dropping columns. - Grouping and aggregation: groupby as split-apply-combine; agg with several statistics and named aggregations; multiple grouping columns; pivot_table as the reproducible form of the Stage 1 pivot; value_counts; cumulative, rolling, and shifted calculations. - Combining tables: merge with how= inner/left/right/outer, validate= for relationship checks, and indicator= for diagnosing row changes; concat for stacking files; index join at recognition level. - Reshaping and tidiness: melt (wide to long) and pivot/pivot_table (long to wide); stack/unstack at recognition level; explode; get_dummies for one-hot encoding; MultiIndex at recognize-and-f…

nodes.label: 3.3 Visualization, workflow, APIs, and automation (source sections 12–15)
nodes.text: 3.3 Visualization, workflow, APIs, and automation (source sections 12–15) - Visualization: figure vs. axes as the one mental model; pandas plotting for a first chart; matplotlib essentials (line/bar/scatter, titles, labels, saving a figure); chart choice by question; seaborn one-liners on tidy data with hue= for grouped comparison; reading a chart critically (truncated axes, chartjunk, misleading bins). - Workflow skills: virtual environments and pip (taught after the browser phase); requirements.txt; Git and GitHub basics (clone, add, commit, push, pull, reading a diff); reading documentation and help; asking AI tools well and verifying the answer by running it; project organization (data / notebooks / outputs, dated file names); notebook fluency including restart-and-run-all before sharing. - APIs and web data: what an API is; HTTP request/response and status codes at concept level; requests.get and reading JSON into dicts/lists; query parameters and API keys kept out of shared notebooks; pagination at concept level; json_normalize from response to DataFrame; scraping awareness through read_html for public tables, with terms and ethics, in one lesson. - Automation and reporting: turning a notebook into a runnable .py script; parameterizing a script at the top; the batch pattern (loop over a folder, clean each file, concat, write one output); scheduled refresh at concept level; automated reporting (Excel/CSV output, a chart image, and a short Markdown/HTML summary in one ru…

nodes.label: 3.4 Python cut list (from the source, kept as scope decisions)
nodes.text: 3.4 Python cut list (from the source, kept as scope decisions) The source demotes the following from Stage 3 core to a later stage, a sidebar, or recognition level only: hand-implemented data structures and sorting algorithms (linked lists, trees, merge sort by hand); OOP depth (inheritance design, dunder methods, properties); decorators, generators, and advanced *args/kwargs; full regular-expression theory; match statements; pytest and unit testing as a module (one awareness lesson on assertions and spot checks instead); NumPy linear-algebra implementation depth; MultiIndex mastery; deep web-scraping frameworks; matplotlib styling internals. The algorithmic consequences of this list are stated explicitly in Section 8. ---

nodes.label: 4. Advanced Core, Part 1 — Statistics, Analytics, and Data-Science Foundations
nodes.text: 4. Advanced Core, Part 1 — Statistics, Analytics, and Data-Science Foundations Source: `syllabus-stats-analytics-ds.md`, sections 1–14 (about 120 items). This inventory is the advanced core for every track and the foundation of the Data Scientist track. Items are in dependency order. The source marks with an opening flag the topics where competitors are weakest — typically formula-first, intuition-light, or skipped — including observational-vs-experimental design, base-rate reasoning, correct confidence-interval interpretation, p-value misreadings, survivorship and missing-not-at-random traps, and Simpson's paradox. Those flags are preserved in substance below because they set teaching priority, not extra topics.

nodes.label: 4.1 Design, description, and visualization judgment (source sections 1–3)
nodes.text: 4.1 Design, description, and visualization judgment (source sections 1–3) - Data types and study design: categorical vs. numerical, discrete vs. continuous; levels of measurement; observational study vs. experiment; confounders and lurking variables; random assignment vs. random sampling as two different jobs; association is not causation at the design stage; units, rows, and grain; data provenance. - Descriptive statistics and distributions: frequency and relative-frequency tables; mean vs. median vs. mode and when each misleads; range, IQR, variance, standard deviation; percentiles, quartiles, and box plots; shape (skewness, modality, symmetry); outlier detection plus the keep/remove judgment; z-scores and standardization; the normal distribution and the empirical rule; binomial, Poisson, uniform, and exponential distributions at recognition level; comparing distributions across groups on center, spread, and shape together. - Visualization judgment: chart choice by question type; what bar, line, scatter, histogram, and box plots are each for; truncated axes, dual axes, and cherry-picked windows; aggregation hiding the story; displaying uncertainty (error bars, bands, sample-size annotation); sorting, labeling, and direct annotation; color discipline including colorblind safety; dashboard vs. exploratory plot.

nodes.label: 4.2 Probability, sampling, and inference (source sections 4–7)
nodes.text: 4.2 Probability, sampling, and inference (source sections 4–7) - Probability foundations: sample spaces, events, addition and complement rules; independent vs. dependent events and the multiplication rule; conditional probability read in both directions; Bayes' theorem as belief updating with base rates first; discrete vs. continuous random variables; expected value; variance of a random variable; law of large numbers at intuition level; permutations and combinations at recognition level. - Sampling and bias: population vs. sample, parameter vs. statistic; simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling; convenience and voluntary-response samples; the bias taxonomy (selection, nonresponse, survivorship, measurement); sampling variability and sampling distributions; the Central Limit Theorem, intuition first; standard error vs. standard deviation; sample size and margin-of-error trade-offs. - Confidence intervals: point vs. interval estimates; correct interpretation of a 95% interval as long-run coverage; intervals for a proportion and for a mean (t-interval); margin of error and what shrinks it; bootstrap intervals for statistics with no neat formula; confidence interval vs. prediction interval. - Hypothesis testing, taught honestly: null and alternative as competing claims; what a p-value is and the three things it is not; significance level and the Type I / Type II trade-off; power and what raises it; one- and two-sample t-tests, paired vs. independent; proport…

nodes.label: 4.3 Experimentation, causation, and regression (source sections 8–10)
nodes.text: 4.3 Experimentation, causation, and regression (source sections 8–10) - A/B testing end to end: from business question to one primary metric; primary, guardrail, and vanity metrics; randomization unit and assignment; sample-size and power analysis before launch; minimum detectable effect as a business choice; running discipline (fixed horizon, no peeking, no mid-test changes); sanity checks (sample-ratio mismatch, instrumentation, seasonality, weekday effects); analyzing means and proportions; ratio metrics and the delta method at recognition level; novelty and primacy effects and long-term holdouts; the ship / no-ship decision memo; Bayesian A/B testing at recognition level. - Correlation vs. causation: the correlation coefficient and its limits; the three rival explanations (reverse causation, confounder, coincidence) as a checklist; spurious correlation and data dredging; Simpson's paradox; the ecological fallacy; regression to the mean; what earns causal language (randomization, natural experiments, difference-in-differences at recognition level, mechanism and dose-response). - Regression as a thinking tool: slope and intercept as a story; least squares and residuals; R² and its limits; reading coefficients with units and baselines; multiple regression as controlling for other variables; categorical predictors and dummy variables; logistic regression (log-odds, odds ratios, predicted probabilities); assumptions and diagnostics; multicollinearity at recognition level; ext…

nodes.label: 4.4 Analytics craft and communication (source sections 11–14)
nodes.text: 4.4 Analytics craft and communication (source sections 11–14) - Metrics, funnels, cohorts, and retention: metric design and gaming resistance; north-star vs. input vs. health metrics; rates vs. counts vs. ratios and denominator choice; funnel analysis (step conversion, drop-off, time between steps); cohort analysis separating age effects from calendar effects; retention curves and churn definitions (logo vs. revenue, voluntary vs. involuntary); segmentation including RFM; customer lifetime value, CAC, and the LTV:CAC ratio; seasonality and year-over-year comparison; anomaly triage (data, real, or us — in that order); instrumentation and event taxonomy basics; data-quality checks inside analysis. - Storytelling and stakeholder communication: starting from the decision, not the dataset; one headline takeaway per chart; narrative structure (context, tension, evidence, recommendation); translating statistical output into business language without losing uncertainty; anticipating hostile questions; documenting method and caveats without burying the answer; agreeing the question and success criteria before analyzing. - Spreadsheet-to-code workflow: the spreadsheet mental model as the bridge to SQL and pandas; cleaning as a first-class step; reproducibility through scripts and notebooks over manual edits; the analyst's loop (question → extract → wrangle → summarize → visualize → communicate); versioning and documenting an analysis; when to stay in a spreadsheet vs. move to code. -…

nodes.label: 4.5 Visualization as a learner skill — extraction note
nodes.text: 4.5 Visualization as a learner skill — extraction note No single source file owns visualization as one inventory; the topic lines are dispersed across Section 1 of this file (Excel charts, Tableau, Power BI), Section 4.1 above (visualization judgment), and the Python visualization topics in Section 3.3. [Recommendation, following the Wave 4 dedupe note] The build should present those lines as one visible visualization strand — chart choice, honest axes and aggregation, uncertainty display, dashboard composition, and tool execution in Excel, Python, Tableau, and Power BI — extracted from the sections above, not researched or listed separately a second time. ---

nodes.label: 5. Advanced Core, Part 2 — How the Core Assembles Before the Track Split
nodes.text: 5. Advanced Core, Part 2 — How the Core Assembles Before the Track Split The advanced core is not a sixth topic list. It is the point in the path where the earlier stages are combined and completed before learners split into the five tracks: - The BI layer of Stage 1 completed at working level: BI concepts (Section 1.6), one BI tool in depth (Tableau in Section 1.7 or Power BI in Section 1.8), and the modeling ideas both tools reward — star schema, grain, relationships, measures vs. columns. - The full statistics and analytics inventory in Section 4, including experimentation, causation, regression, product-analytics craft, and stakeholder communication. - The AI-era concepts module in Section 7 (retrieval-augmented generation and agents as literacy, evaluation basics, and evaluating "chat with your data" products), placed here because it assumes SQL, Python, and a formed verification habit. - A cross-tool end-to-end case in the analyst's loop from Section 4.4: one question carried through extraction, wrangling, summarization, visualization, and a written recommendation. Project and portfolio design for that case, and for each track's capstone, is owned by the projects research (Wave 2B) and is not listed here. Track entry expectations follow directly: the Data Analyst track deepens Sections 1, 4.4, and the BI layer; the Data Scientist track deepens Section 4 and Part B of Section 6; the Data Engineer and Analytics Engineer tracks deepen Part A of Section 6; the ML/AI Engine…

nodes.label: 6. Specialized Tracks — Data Engineering, Machine Learning / Deep Learning, Applied AI
nodes.text: 6. Specialized Tracks — Data Engineering, Machine Learning / Deep Learning, Applied AI Source: `syllabus-de-ml-ai.md` — Part A (Data Engineering, A0–A12, serving the Data Engineer and Analytics Engineer tracks) and Part B (Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Applied AI, B0–B12, serving the Data Scientist and ML/AI Engineer tracks), plus the source's capstone shapes and its hype-vs-fundamentals flags, preserved in substance at the end of this section.

nodes.label: 6.1 Data Engineering (source Part A)
nodes.text: 6.1 Data Engineering (source Part A) - A0 Ground rules: what a data engineer owns vs. analysts and data scientists; the data lifecycle (generate → ingest → store → transform → serve); batch vs. streaming as a business decision with a price attached. - A1 Ingestion: extracting from REST APIs (auth, pagination, rate limits); reading CSV, JSON, Parquet, and Excel defensively; incremental extraction (updated_at watermarks, change data capture at concept level); failure modes (retries, idempotent loads, dead-letter handling). - A2 Data modeling: entities, keys, and relationships in plain language; normalization (1NF–3NF) and when to break it; dimensional modeling (fact vs. dimension); star and snowflake schemas; slowly changing dimensions (Type 1 vs. Type 2); naming and grain discipline. - A3 Storage: OLTP vs. OLAP and row vs. columnar stores; data warehouse concepts; data lake concepts (object storage, schema-on-read); lakehouse and open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg; ACID, time travel, schema enforcement); file-format trade-offs (CSV vs. Parquet vs. JSON); partitioning and clustering basics. - A4 ETL/ELT and pipeline design: ETL vs. ELT and why ELT won in cloud warehouses; pipeline anatomy (extract → stage → transform → load → serve); staging layers and the medallion pattern (bronze/silver/gold); full vs. incremental loads, upserts, and merges; backfills and safe reprocessing; idempotency as a design rule. - A5 Batch pipelines in Python: pandas for pipeline work; co…

nodes.label: 6.2 Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Applied AI (source Part B)
nodes.text: 6.2 Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Applied AI (source Part B) - B0 Framing: what ML is for (prediction under uncertainty) and what it is not; problem framing (target, unit of analysis, the decision the model feeds); classification vs. regression vs. ranking vs. forecasting; the baseline-first rule; data availability and label-quality audit. - B1 Workflow and honest evaluation: train/validation/test splits; data leakage (target leakage and train/test contamination), promoted ahead of algorithms in the source; cross-validation (k-fold, stratified, time-based); bias–variance and over/underfitting diagnosis; error analysis before model shopping. Framing and metrics material here is cross-referenced from Section 4 in the build, not retaught as a separate statistics block. - B2 Metrics per problem type: regression metrics (MAE, RMSE, R²) and when each misleads; accuracy and its failure on imbalanced data; precision, recall, F1, and the threshold trade-off; ROC/AUC and precision–recall curves; the confusion matrix as a communication tool; business-cost framing of errors. - B3 Supervised learning, core algorithms: linear regression; feature scaling; logistic regression; regularization (L1/L2 in plain terms); decision trees; random forests; gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM class); k-NN and SVM at awareness level; Naive Bayes at awareness level; time-series forecasting basics (trend/seasonality, lag features, honest backtesting by time). - B4 Feature engineering: missing-valu…

nodes.label: 6.3 Hype vs. fundamentals flags (preserved from the source)
nodes.text: 6.3 Hype vs. fundamentals flags (preserved from the source) The source flags the following as oversold in competitor syllabi, and this inventory follows its placement decisions: agents as a starting topic (here they sit after APIs, evaluation, and data plumbing); fine-tuning LLMs early (here a decision inside B10, not a default skill); prompt engineering as a standalone career skill (here one layer of B10, whose durable core is evaluation and structured output); real-time-everything streaming (here one awareness section, A10, with an explicit when-not-to item); deep learning before classical ML (here B3 precedes B8); and certificate-shaped breadth, one course per cloud service (here A11 teaches the transferable pattern — storage, orchestration, cost — on one cloud). The source flags the following as under-taught, and this inventory deliberately promotes them: data leakage (B1, before algorithms); idempotency, backfills, and reprocessing (A4, A6); data quality as its own discipline (A9); cost literacy (A3, A11, B10); evaluation of LLM applications (B10); reading and debugging other people's pipelines and models (B1, B7); and dimensional-modeling depth (A2). ---

nodes.label: 7. The AI-Era Layer, Threaded Through the Path
nodes.text: 7. The AI-Era Layer, Threaded Through the Path Cross-reference only. The skills taxonomy, the incumbent-coverage evidence, and the placement map are owned by `waves/wave2-c-ai-era-layer.md`; this section records where that layer lands against the topic lists above, so the build threads it instead of appending it as one late module. All placement statements in this section are [Recommendation] from that file. - Before Stage 1 — a short primer, no new tool skills. What a large language model is in one plain model (a system that predicts plausible output from context, which is why it is useful and why it invents); the prompting habit loop (task → context → references/examples → evaluate → iterate); privacy rules with concrete never-paste categories; and the course-wide rule that AI output is a draft until verified. - Inside Stage 1 (Section 1). After tables and core formulas are learned unaided: spreadsheet assistance — generating formulas from descriptions, explaining inherited formulas, generating charts by description; interaction modes taught explicitly (explain-only → propose/plan → direct edit on a copy); in-cell AI text functions for categorization and summarization with a hand-checked sample before scaling; a trap exercise with a planted aggregation error. Gate [Recommendation]: an unaided formula-reading check before AI-assisted spreadsheet work is assessed. - Inside Stage 2 (Section 2). After SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, and JOIN are learned unaided: natural-language-to-S…

nodes.label: 8. Algorithms and Complexity — Extracted Inventory and Scope Decision
nodes.text: 8. Algorithms and Complexity — Extracted Inventory and Scope Decision This is the thinnest inventory in the package, and this section says so plainly rather than implying coverage that the sources do not contain. The Wave 4 dedupe pass (gap G) found no dedicated algorithm inventory in the corpus comparable to the SQL inventory: algorithmic material exists only in scattered form inside the syllabus files. Everything in Section 8.1 is extracted from those files. Section 8.2 is the explicit scope decision for the build. No topic is presented in Section 8.1 as sourced unless it appears in a syllabus file named there.

nodes.label: 8.1 What the syllabus files actually contain
nodes.text: 8.1 What the syllabus files actually contain - Algorithm families as modeling tools (`syllabus-de-ml-ai.md`, Part B): the supervised, unsupervised, and deep-learning families listed in Sections 6.2 (B3, B5, B8) — linear and logistic regression, trees, forests, boosting, k-NN, SVM, Naive Bayes, k-means and other clustering, PCA, and the neural-network family. These are taught as models to frame, evaluate, and explain — not as algorithms to implement from scratch. - Sorting and searching as used operations (`syllabus-python.md`, sections 4–5; `syllabus-sql.md`, sections 3 and 14): sorting with key= and lambda; sorting and ranking in SQL (ORDER BY, ranking window functions); predicting sort and join costs at the level of the SQL performance topics (join algorithms — nested loop, hash, merge — at awareness level; index and B-tree mental models). The operation is taught; implementing a sort is not. - Data-structure choice as judgment (`syllabus-python.md`, section 5): lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets, choosing the right structure for a task, and set operations for membership questions. Structures are consumed through Python and SQL, not implemented. - Counting at recognition level (`syllabus-stats-analytics-ds.md`, section 4): permutations and combinations as denominators for probability sanity checks. - Recursive and iterative patterns in data work (`syllabus-sql.md`, section 6; `syllabus-python.md`, section 4): recursive CTEs for hierarchies and date spines; loops, compreh…

nodes.label: 8.2 Scope decision for Data From Zero
nodes.text: 8.2 Scope decision for Data From Zero [Recommendation — explicit scope decision, stated here because the sources leave the gap open] 1. The core path (Stages 1–3, advanced core) teaches algorithmic thinking in context only: choosing a data structure, stating grain before computing, preferring vectorized and set-based operations over row loops, reading a join or sort cost at awareness level, and recognizing when a problem's size changes the right tool (spreadsheet → SQL → pandas → Spark, in the order the path itself teaches them). No Big-O formalism beyond that size intuition, and no from-scratch implementation of sorting, searching, or classic data structures, is required in the core path. 2. The ML/AI track teaches algorithm families as models (Section 6.2), with evaluation and leakage discipline as the graded core — not algorithm implementation. 3. A standalone algorithms and complexity module — formal complexity notation, sorting and searching implementations, classic data-structure implementations, and software-engineering interview patterns — is out of scope for this inventory and for the current build. If it is ever added, it belongs as a separate optional computer-science track, consistent with the Python source's cut list, and it must be commissioned as its own inventory rather than inferred from this file. 4. Builders must not present Data From Zero as covering a general algorithms curriculum. Any page, roadmap node, or marketing line implying one exists would be in…

nodes.label: 9. Certification-Alignment Cross-Reference Note
nodes.text: 9. Certification-Alignment Cross-Reference Note Cross-reference only. What each certification tests, its domains and weightings, and the full cross-certification topic matrix are owned by `waves/wave2-d-certification-map.md`; hiring-task readiness is a separate definition owned by Wave 2A. This note records only which parts of this inventory each credential's blueprint touches, so a learner can be told honestly what a completed stage does and does not align with. No price, pass mark, or weighting is restated here. - Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate — touches Stages 1–3 and Section 4.4: framing a question, preparing and cleaning data in spreadsheets and SQL, analyzing, sharing findings with visualizations and dashboards, introductory Python for analysis, and an end-to-end case study. It does not center deep statistics, machine learning, pipelines, or cloud platforms. - Microsoft Office Specialist: Excel Associate (MO-210) — touches Stage 1 only: workbook and worksheet management, cells and ranges, structured tables with sorting and filtering, core formulas and functions, and charts. The source certification map treats Associate as the Excel block's floor; PivotTables and lookups in Section 1.3 sit past it, in the Expert direction. - Microsoft PL-300 (Power BI Data Analyst) — touches the BI layer (Sections 1.6–1.8) as a complete workflow: prepare data in Power Query, model facts and dimensions with a date table, calculate in DAX, visualize and analyze, then deplo…

nodes.label: 1. The method in one page
nodes.text: 1. The method in one page Data From Zero is built against four documented failure modes in incumbent data courses: 1. Tutorial hell / the illusion of competence. [Sourced — pedagogy research] Learners finish course after course, follow every tutorial successfully, then freeze at a blank file — because the instructor made every decision (structure, names, order, debugging) and the learner practiced executing, not deciding. 2. The transfer gap. [Sourced — pedagogy research] Learners complete SQL, Python, or analytics courses, then cannot clean a messy real export, join tables that do not match a tutorial's clean schema, or answer an open-ended business question. 3. Drop-off from being stuck and from life, not from difficulty. [Sourced — pedagogy research] Completion research summarized in the research record finds non-completers cite lack of time far ahead of lost motivation or difficulty, and that dropout concentrates in the first two weeks, with speed of early completion predicting finishing better than demographics. 4. Math anxiety as an avoidance barrier. [Sourced — pedagogy research] Anxiety about mathematics drives avoidance rather than reflecting inability; platforms that front-load formulas lose learners before the applied version appears. Ten method stances answer those failures. They are stated here once, as policy; the rest of this file operationalizes them: 1. Production over recognition. No fill-in-the-blank exercise is ever a lesson's terminal exercise. Every les…

nodes.label: 2. The canonical lesson template — seven sections
nodes.text: 2. The canonical lesson template — seven sections Total target length: 15–20 minutes for a standard lesson. [Recommendation] Lessons introducing a genuinely new mental model (first join, first groupby, first hypothesis test) may run to 25 minutes [Recommendation]; lessons extending a known pattern should run shorter, not longer. For calibration only: the research record describes incumbent lesson lengths of roughly 10–15 minutes for one video-plus-exercise platform and typically 5–10 minutes for one text-plus-code platform [Sourced]. Those figures describe incumbents; they do not set this site's target. | # | Section | Time [Recommendation] | Contents | Why it exists | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Recall opener | 1–2 min | 2–3 prompts drawn from earlier lessons — not only the previous one — answered from memory before scrolling, with click-to-reveal answers. At least one prompt is a *production* prompt ("write the formula / query / line that does X"), never only multiple-choice recognition. | Retrieval practice is the highest-evidence feature a static page can ship. Placing it first also tells the learner honestly what has and has not stuck, before new material covers the gap. | | 2 | The job question | 1 min | One concrete question in business language, with the data visible: a small table, a sheet excerpt, or a chart. No syntax yet. The lesson's promise is stated as the answer the learner will be able to produce by the end. | Hiring tests judgment on business-flavored promp…

nodes.label: 2.1 Rules that apply to every lesson, in every domain
nodes.text: 2.1 Rules that apply to every lesson, in every domain - One new idea per lesson. [Recommendation, grounded in Sourced cognitive-load material] If a lesson needs two new ideas, it is two lessons. Combining a new concept with a new tool feature doubles intrinsic load at exactly the moment the learner has no schema for either. - Name the pattern, not just the syntax. [Recommendation] After the blank-start task, the lesson names the reusable pattern in plain language ("filter, then aggregate, then rank inside each group"), so the learner files the lesson under a *move*, not under a keyword. Interview-prep sources in the research record give the same advice: name the pattern after solving, then re-solve after the data is mutated. - Every exercise states its grain, denominator, or expected output shape before the learner starts. [Recommendation] Silent ambiguity about output shape is the most common cause of "correct work, wrong answer" in the hiring-task research. - Worked examples come in pairs for any pattern that must transfer. [Recommendation — see the mixed-evidence note in Section 1] Section 4 is the first example; Section 5, before fading bites, functions as the second. A lesson whose pattern is known to be confused with a neighboring pattern must instead use Section 4 for a side-by-side contrast pair (see the Statistics and SQL notes in Section 3). - The solution is never the first thing on the page. [Recommendation] Solutions, half-solutions, and reveal answers sit behin…

nodes.label: 3. Per-domain anatomy
nodes.text: 3. Per-domain anatomy Each domain keeps the Section 2 template and changes four things: the canonical visual, the worked-example progression across a topic, the exercise ladder, and the framing ritual the blank-start task requires. Ladders have five rungs; all rung designs, progressions, and rituals in this section are [Recommendation] unless marked [Sourced]. Topic coverage itself lives in 02-syllabus-inventory and is not reprinted here.

nodes.label: 3.1 Excel — spreadsheets first, BI concepts introduced through the sheet
nodes.text: 3.1 Excel — spreadsheets first, BI concepts introduced through the sheet Canonical visual: The sheet itself, annotated in place. For formulas: a small grid showing the formula in one cell and the values it becomes when copied down and across, with locked and moving parts in two colors. For PivotTables: the source range on the left and the pivoted result on the right, with arrows from field to area (rows / columns / values / filters). Never a screenshot of a ribbon menu as the "explanation" — menus change between versions; grid behavior does not. Worked-example progression — topic: lookups (the highest-tested Excel skill in the hiring-task research [Sourced]): 1. *Fully worked:* Bring a unit price from a reference sheet into an orders sheet by product code, where every code matches. Narration covers: why exact match is chosen deliberately, which range must stay fixed when the formula is copied, and how the result is verified (spot-check two codes by eye; total the extended amounts and reconcile). 2. *Faded:* Same task on a new file where the setup and first rows are done; the learner writes the lookup for the remaining segment and copies it correctly. One code has no match; the half-solution hint asks what the output *should* show for that row before offering any formula help. 3. *Contrast pair:* Two completed lookups side by side — one that handles the missing code deliberately (a readable "not found" result) and one that leaves a raw error value in the output column — with…

nodes.label: 3.2 SQL — one complete block, organized by pattern in its second half
nodes.text: 3.2 SQL — one complete block, organized by pattern in its second half Canonical visual: A row-flow diagram. Source tables are drawn as row stacks; each clause of the query is a gate the rows pass through — rows drop out at the filter gate, rows merge into group buckets at the aggregation gate, buckets are labeled with their computed values, then sorted. The lesson on query execution order uses this same diagram, so the visual and the execution model are one object, not two. Worked-example progression — topic: top-N per group: 1. *Fully worked:* "Top product by revenue in each category." Narration in fixed order: state the grain first (one row per category), aggregate to one row per product, rank products inside each category, keep the top rank, and state the tie policy out loud (what happens if two products tie — and which ranking function that choice implies). Verification: count the output rows and confirm it equals the number of categories. 2. *Faded:* "Second order for each customer." Aggregation and ranking steps are given; the learner writes the final selection step and the tie handling. The dataset contains a customer with only one order — the hint asks what that customer should contribute to the output before any syntax help is offered. 3. *Messy re-solve:* The step-1 problem again, but the orders table now contains duplicate rows and a missing category value. The naive query returns an inflated revenue figure. The task is to find why, repair it, and write two plain…

nodes.label: 3.3 Python — core language, then pandas as the center of gravity
nodes.text: 3.3 Python — core language, then pandas as the center of gravity Canonical visual: For core Python, a state trace: a small table showing each variable's value after each line runs, so a loop or function call is a visible change of state rather than a paragraph of prose. For pandas, the table transformation itself: the input frame drawn beside the output frame, with the rows or columns kept, dropped, grouped, or created highlighted — the same row-flow idea as SQL, drawn on dataframes. Worked-example progression — topic: grouping and aggregation in pandas: 1. *Fully worked:* Total revenue by category from a small sales frame. Narration covers: inspect the frame first (shape, types, missing values) before any computation; group, then aggregate with several named metrics in one pass; verify by reconciling the grouped total against the ungrouped total. 2. *Faded:* Share of orders by channel. Grouping is given; the learner writes the normalization step and must state whether missing channel values are inside or outside the denominator — and why. Denominator treatment in share-of-total is an explicit interview attention point [Sourced — hiring-task research]. 3. *Trap example:* Fill missing values using each row's *own group* average, shown next to the incorrect version that uses the single overall average. The two results differ visibly on the worked data; the narration explains that broadcasting a group-level value back onto rows is a distinct move from aggregating, with its own…

nodes.label: 3.4 Statistics / Analytics — the advanced core's first half
nodes.text: 3.4 Statistics / Analytics — the advanced core's first half Canonical visual: A picture of data, always before any formula. A distribution drawn as dots or bars that visibly splits when a filter is applied; a confidence interval drawn as a range over repeated samples; an A/B result drawn as two distributions with their overlap shaded. Formulas, where they appear at all, appear *after* the picture, labeled as the shorthand for what the picture shows, with an optional depth layer for learners who want the derivation. Worked-example progression — topic: "is this difference real?" (the A/B / two-group comparison): 1. *Fully worked, picture only:* Two groups' results plotted; the narration walks through a fixed diagnostic order — is the signal real (any tracking change, outage, holiday, or definition change?), then segment (platform, region, new vs. returning), then locate the driver, then state a hypothesis. No test statistic is computed in this first pass. [Order of operations Sourced — hiring-task research] 2. *Worked with numbers:* The same structure on new data, now adding the interval and the plain-language reading of it: what the interval says, and — explicitly — what a p-value is *not*. The deliverable includes the three-sentence spoken explanation the learner would give a non-technical stakeholder. 3. *Contrast pair:* Two analyses of the same experiment side by side: one that stopped early on the first encouraging result, and one that ran a full weekly cycle with primary…

nodes.label: 3.5 Data Engineering / Machine Learning / AI — the track layer
nodes.text: 3.5 Data Engineering / Machine Learning / AI — the track layer What changes at track level: The unit of a lesson is no longer a single operation; it is a *stage of a system* — one ingestion step, one transformation with tests, one stage of a modeling workflow. The worked example therefore shows a whole small system first (a handful of boxes or steps, end to end, on toy-scale data) and then zooms into one stage per lesson. A learner who has only ever seen stages in isolation cannot answer track-level interview questions, which are about how stages interact: leakage between stages, what breaks when a rerun happens, what happens when the source changes shape [Sourced — hiring-task research]. Canonical visual: For DE: a pipeline diagram with data volumes and failure points marked on the arrows, not just boxes — the arrow where duplicates enter, the arrow where a schema change lands. For ML: the workflow drawn as a one-way street with a wall between the data used to fit and the data used to judge, so leakage is a visible crossing of the wall rather than an abstract warning. For applied AI lessons: the same discipline — input, retrieval or tool step, model step, verification step — drawn as stages with the checkable artifact each stage produces. Worked-example progression — topic: DE, ingest and clean a messy file into a trustworthy table: 1. *Fully worked:* Ingest a small file with a nested field, inconsistent keys, and duplicate records. Narration covers: profile before transfor…

nodes.label: 4. Illustrative end-to-end topic: SQL joins
nodes.text: 4. Illustrative end-to-end topic: SQL joins [Recommendation — a worked illustration of the system above, not a sourced claim.] Topic: SQL joins, lessons 1–4 of the topic, topic checkpoint in lesson 5's slot. - Lesson 1 (inner joins): Recall opener reaches back to filtering and aggregation. Visual: two row stacks aligning on a key, unmatched rows visibly falling away. Worked example answers "orders with their customer names" with grain stated and row count verified against the orders table. Faded example changes the table pair. Blank-start task adds a duplicate key on the customer side — the row count check fails, and finding out why *is* the lesson's real content. - Lesson 2 (finding rows with no match): The visual extends the same diagram — now the unmatched rows are the ones kept, highlighted. The contrast pair (the two join shapes side by side on identical data) does the teaching; the blank-start task is "customers who have never ordered," with one customer whose only order was canceled, forcing a stated decision about what counts. - Lesson 3 (join before vs. after aggregating): A critique lesson. A plausible query inflates revenue by joining two many-sided tables first; the learner diagnoses it, repairs it by aggregating before joining, and writes the two-sentence metric explanation. - Lesson 4 (multi-table, messy): Three tables, duplicates, a missing key value. Framing ritual, blank start, verification against a hand-computed total for one customer. - Topic checkpoint:…

nodes.label: 5. Checkpoint design
nodes.text: 5. Checkpoint design *All numeric thresholds, frequencies, and time limits in this section are [Recommendation] unless marked otherwise. No platform's internal pass threshold is claimed anywhere in this section, because none of the pages opened during the research states one in a form that generalizes.*

nodes.label: 5.1 Three checkpoint sizes, three different jobs
nodes.text: 5.1 Three checkpoint sizes, three different jobs | Checkpoint | Frequency [Recommendation] | Contents | Job | |---|---|---|---| | Lesson exit ticket | Every lesson (template Section 7) | One closed-book recall item on the lesson + one spot-the-flaw item + the verifiable ability self-rating | Catches same-day illusion of competence while repair is still cheap. | | Topic checkpoint | Every 3–5 lessons, at the end of each named pattern or topic (e.g., "joins," "groupby," "two-group comparisons") | A mixed set: items from *all* lessons in the topic, in shuffled order, with the pattern unnamed — the learner must first decide which move applies. At least one blank-start task and one critique task. | Tests selection, not just execution. A learner who can execute each pattern when it is named but cannot choose between them has recognition, not skill. | | Block exit checkpoint | Once per block (Excel, SQL, Python, advanced core, each track) | The domain's rung-5 task under hiring-shaped conditions: timed, on messy data, with a short written narration (assumptions, pattern chosen, validation performed) submitted alongside the work. | Certifies the block in the shape hiring will test it. This is the only checkpoint whose result should be described to the learner as "interview-shaped." | One incumbent analogue is worth naming: a help-center page cited in the research record describes a unit assignment as complete only once the learner reaches the required level in *all* skills in the un…

nodes.label: 5.2 Pass rules
nodes.text: 5.2 Pass rules - Pass = production, unaided, on unseen data. [Recommendation] A checkpoint item counts as passed only if the learner produced the answer from a blank start, on data they have not seen in a worked example, without opening the full-solution layer of the help stack. Using a concept hint is permitted and noted; using the half-solution caps the item at "passed with support," which does not satisfy a gate. - Threshold: all critical items, most items overall. [Recommendation] Designate, per checkpoint, the small set of *critical* items — the ones whose failure invalidates downstream work (grain errors in SQL, reference errors in Excel, group-scope errors in pandas, definition errors in Statistics, leakage in ML). Rule: 100% of critical items and at least 4 of 5 items overall to pass a topic checkpoint; 100% of critical items at a block exit, with no compensation from other sections. Rationale: an average-based threshold lets a learner pass while carrying exactly the one misconception the next block assumes away. These numbers are design choices for Data From Zero, stated so they can be debated and changed in one place; they are not research findings. - Two attempts before intervention, then a changed strategy — not a third identical attempt. [Recommendation] Attempt 1: full checkpoint. Attempt 2: only the failed items, after completing the repair loop in Section 6. If attempt 2 fails on the same item type, the learner is routed to a *different representation* of the…

nodes.label: 5.3 What checkpoints must never do
nodes.text: 5.3 What checkpoints must never do - Never gate progress on a recognition item (multiple choice, fill-in-the-blank) alone. [Recommendation] - Never report a single percentage as the learner's state. Report the ability list: which verifiable abilities are confirmed, which are passed-with-support, which are in repair. [Recommendation] - Never let a streak, point total, or completion count substitute for a passed blank-start task. Completion-contingent rewards optimize for lesson completion, and platforms then serve easier content to protect the metric [Sourced risk — pedagogy research].

nodes.label: 5.4 Note: checkpoint resistance to AI-generated answers
nodes.text: 5.4 Note: checkpoint resistance to AI-generated answers [Recommendation — design note closing a gap flagged in the verification wave; no new research is claimed here.] Data From Zero is a free static site with no accounts and no server-side grading, so its checkpoints are self-checked by design — a learner who wants to deceive the site is only deceiving their own ability list. The design should still make honest production the path of least resistance, and make pasted answers visibly insufficient: 1. Unseen, mutated data. Checkpoint tasks use data the learner has not seen in a worked example, with surface features changed. A generated answer to the *named* pattern still has to be adapted to *this* data — and the adaptation is the skill. 2. Framing before output. Every checkpoint task requires the framing line first (grain, definition, contract, expected shape). A pasted solution without a correct framing line fails on the Framing bucket (Section 6), in the learner's own self-check. 3. Verification as a scored step. The learner must show the check — the reconciled total, the row count against the grain statement, the baseline comparison — not only the answer. Generated output rarely ships with a check that matches this dataset. 4. Narration at block exits. The written narration (assumptions, pattern chosen, validation performed) is personal to the attempt. It is also the exact artifact hiring's live rounds will demand unaided, which is the honest argument to put on the page:…

nodes.label: 6. Failure diagnosis and spaced review
nodes.text: 6. Failure diagnosis and spaced review

nodes.label: 6.1 Four failure buckets, four different repairs
nodes.text: 6.1 Four failure buckets, four different repairs Every failed checkpoint item returns a *diagnosis*, not just a mark. [Recommendation] Feedback classifies the failure into exactly one of four buckets, because each bucket has a different repair: 1. Concept — the wrong move was chosen (wrong join type, wrong denominator, wrong metric). *Repair:* re-study the canonical visual and the contrast pair for the confused patterns, then a faded example. 2. Execution — the right move, wrongly carried out (a syntax slip, a copied formula that drifted, a misordered clause). *Repair:* two rung-2 (Complete) exercises on the same pattern, then retry. 3. Framing — the work is internally correct but answers a different question (wrong grain, unstated tie policy, undefined metric, output in the wrong shape). *Repair:* rewrite only the framing line and the verification step for the failed task, explain in one sentence what the original framing got wrong, then retry the full task. This bucket exists because the hiring-task research found framing failures to be the most common *silent* failure mode — the work runs, and is wrong. 4. Verification — the answer is wrong and the learner's own check should have caught it (totals do not reconcile, row count contradicts the grain statement). *Repair:* a dedicated verification drill — three short tasks whose only job is to find the planted discrepancy — before any retry. A learner who cannot check work cannot safely work unsupervised, in any domain. Retry…

nodes.label: 6.2 Spaced review, attached to checkpoints
nodes.text: 6.2 Spaced review, attached to checkpoints - Each lesson's material re-enters the recall openers and mixed review sets on a fixed schedule. The intervals are [Recommendation]; the principle is [Sourced — pedagogy research: the spacing effect is among the most replicated findings in experimental psychology, and a simple fixed schedule captures most of the benefit of algorithmic scheduling]. Data From Zero's fixed schedule: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 21 days after the lesson is passed. [Recommendation — these exact intervals are a design choice.] - A review item failed twice returns its lesson to "needs repair" status and inserts the Section 6.1 loop for that item's failure bucket. [Recommendation] Review is therefore not a separate game layered over the curriculum; it is the mechanism that can reopen a closed lesson. - Block exit checkpoints sample earlier blocks, not only their own: the Python exit includes SQL-pattern translations; the advanced-core exit includes one Excel- or SQL-shaped task. [Recommendation] Hiring demands the same pattern across tools, so the checkpoints must too. - Implementation on a static site: [Recommendation] the schedule renders as a "review today" page generated from the roadmap structure, plus a printable/downloadable review checklist; progress is stored in the browser only. No accounts, no server scheduler. ---

nodes.label: 7. Visual-teaching integration (summary)
nodes.text: 7. Visual-teaching integration (summary) The full technique catalog, build costs, and asset priorities live in 04-ui-ux-lessons. This section is the playbook-level summary lesson authors need: which visual each domain's lessons use, and the house rules every visual obeys.

nodes.label: 7.1 Per-domain canonical visuals (selection)
nodes.text: 7.1 Per-domain canonical visuals (selection) | Domain | Canonical visual | What it makes obvious before syntax | |---|---|---| | Excel | The annotated sheet grid in place: formula cell plus the values it becomes when copied, locked vs. moving parts in two colors; source range → pivoted result with field-to-area arrows | Reference behavior; what a pivot does to rows | | SQL — joins | Two small tables, arrows pairing rows in the middle, result table building row by row on the right, persistent row-count badge | Pairing as the mechanism; join types as policies about unpaired rows | | SQL — grouping / windows | Row-flow gates (filter → group buckets → sort) and a table stepper: active partition outlined, current frame shaded, computed value appearing as the frame covers each row | GROUP BY collapses rows; window functions preserve them | | Python | State trace (variable values after each line) and name-and-arrow object diagrams; DataFrame as a labeled grid with an index rail | Execution as visible state change; aliasing; selection and grouping on frames | | Statistics | A picture of data first: distributions that split under a filter, running-frequency / running-mean traces, sampling-distribution builder, two-group overlap picture | Probability, expectation, spread, and significance intuition before any formula | | Regression / ML | Scatterplot with a draggable line and residual sticks; scatterplot regions → histogram split finder → growing tree with synchronized partitions; a c…

nodes.label: 7.2 House rules for every visual
nodes.text: 7.2 House rules for every visual [Recommendation throughout, synthesized from the visual-teaching research; the underlying dual-channel and split-attention principles are Sourced.] 1. Sequence: show the data moving first, name the mechanism while it is visible, show syntax or formula last, then let the learner change one thing and predict first. No hard concept is introduced by syntax or formula alone. 2. Predict-before-reveal. Before any animation or stepper advances, ask what will happen. Reveal on click. Watching becomes retrieval practice. 3. One shared visual grammar. Tables always look like tables, partitions always use the same wall style, groups always use the same buckets, a filter always uses the same chip style — across Excel, SQL, Python, and statistics. The bucket diagram for grouping is deliberately the *same artwork* in Excel pivots, SQL GROUP BY, and pandas groupby, with different syntax captions: one operation, three syntaxes. 4. Color with a job, never decoration. One color per table, per class, per partition, held constant through a whole lesson and stated in a legend. Never encode meaning in color alone — pair it with labels or patterns. 5. Small, rigged data. Every teaching dataset is tiny and deliberately loaded: a NULL key, a tie, an outlier, a duplicate — each odd row exists to make exactly one distinction visible. Realistic messy data belongs in projects; canonical visuals need data designed like a demonstration. 6. Step controls over autoplay. Play,…

nodes.label: 8. Vietnamese-learner rules
nodes.text: 8. Vietnamese-learner rules *This section owns all /vi/ rules for the package (per the Wave 4 dedupe map). It applies to lessons written under this playbook and to the /vi/ lesson template slots. Confidence: the Excel localization facts in Section 8.4 are [Sourced] from the pages named there and were confirmed in the verification wave; terminology traps, format manifestations, and code-switching patterns are curriculum judgment from the research record, presented as such — not as measured facts.*

nodes.label: 8.1 The core decision: teach in Vietnamese, work in English
nodes.text: 8.1 The core decision: teach in Vietnamese, work in English The design problem, in one pattern from the research record: a Vietnam data job posting opened during the research is written in English, lists Python (pandas), SQL, and JSON / CSV / API skills, and then adds — as a separate requirement — good communication skills in Vietnamese and English [Sourced]. The tools, keywords, and interview surface are English; the workplace conversation — understanding a manager's request, explaining a finding — happens in Vietnamese, English, or a mix. A local provider in the same research wraps an English-language global certificate with Vietnamese-language live instruction; the wrapper is the product the /vi/ section should be, except free, self-paced, and built in from the start. The dual-track rule: [Recommendation] 1. /vi/ explains, EN names. Explanations, analogies, worked-example narration, and checkpoint questions are in Vietnamese on /vi/ pages. Every technical name — function, keyword, library, job title — stays in its English working form, introduced once with a Vietnamese gloss and then used in English thereafter. 2. EN pages never assume Vietnamese. The root (EN) path is complete on its own. The /vi/ path is not a translation of it; it is the same sequence re-taught with Vietnamese scaffolding, Vietnamese-context examples, and extra bridges where English itself is the obstacle (Section 8.3). 3. No bilingual pages. One language per page. Terms are language-neutral anchors th…

nodes.label: 8.2 Terminology: the three-bucket rule and the glossary
nodes.text: 8.2 Terminology: the three-bucket rule and the glossary Bucket A — Always retain in English, never translate in running text. SQL keywords (`SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`), Excel function names (`SUM`, `VLOOKUP`, `XLOOKUP`, `COUNTIF`), Python keywords and library names (`pandas`, `DataFrame`, `groupby`, `merge`), file formats (CSV, JSON), and error names (`#N/A`, `KeyError`, `NULL`). These are typed, searched, and read verbatim at work. Translating them in prose teaches a word the learner will never see on screen. Bucket B — Retain in English, gloss in Vietnamese on first use per lesson. Concept nouns that are also job-market keywords: *dataset, dashboard, insight, stakeholder, churn, conversion rate, outlier, median, distribution, hypothesis*. Format on /vi/ pages: English term in bold, Vietnamese gloss in parentheses on first use, English term alone after that. On EN pages: a one-line plain-English definition instead. Bucket C — Translate freely into Vietnamese. Instructional and connective language: verbs of action in exercises (calculate, compare, check, explain), business-context nouns that are not technical terms (customer, order, delivery, branch, month-end close), and all analogy / storytelling text. This is where Vietnamese does its real work — carrying reasoning, not labels. What not to do: - Do not translate a Bucket A term in a heading, button, or checkpoint answer. A checkpoint that accepts a translated keyword trains the wrong reflex. - Do not gloss the…

nodes.label: 8.3 How /vi/ pages differ beyond translation — seven ways, and only these
nodes.text: 8.3 How /vi/ pages differ beyond translation — seven ways, and only these So the two paths stay the same path, a /vi/ lesson differs from its EN counterpart in exactly these seven ways: [Recommendation] 1. An English-terms preview box at the top. The 3–6 Bucket A/B terms the lesson will use, each with its gloss, before the lesson body — so working memory at the moment the new *concept* arrives is spent on the concept, not the vocabulary. EN pages get a plainer "key terms" box with definitions — same slot, different job. 2. Worked examples narrated one step slower, with the "why" in Vietnamese. Fuller narration between steps, the mistake a beginner is about to make named *before* the step that triggers it, and a "check yourself" pause after each worked example. Local providers compete on exactly this human accompaniment; a free self-paced site bakes the accompaniment into the page. 3. Code-switching taught as a skill, not treated as a failure. Worked examples follow the daily job loop: a request in Vietnamese (a manager-style ask) → the solution in English-named tools → a Vietnamese summary sentence the learner could actually send. Each lesson ends with a "say it at work" line — Vietnamese with embedded English terms — rehearsing the reporting register, not only the tool register. A recurring /vi/-only exercise type drills reading real-shaped English error messages and documentation paragraphs: what it means, and what to do. 4. Localized examples replace, not decorate. The *s…

nodes.label: 8.4 Format traps — including the Excel correction
nodes.text: 8.4 Format traps — including the Excel correction Excel function names are NOT localized for Vietnamese. [Sourced, confirmed in the verification wave] A detailed explainer on Excel across languages, opened during the research, lists the languages for which Microsoft translated function names (French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Polish, Russian, and others) and explicitly lists Vietnamese among the languages not translated. Workbook files store formulas internally in English; in Vietnamese Excel the menus and help may be Vietnamese, but the learner still types `=SUM(...)` and `=VLOOKUP(...)`. Any course material that invents Vietnamese function names is teaching fiction. All Data From Zero formulas are therefore published in English names, with no translated formula variants anywhere. [Recommendation] The real trap is the list separator and the CSV locale. [Sourced mechanism; Vietnam-specific manifestations are curriculum judgment] The same explainer confirms the mechanism: where the comma is the decimal mark, Excel uses the semicolon as the argument separator (its worked examples are European); and CSV field and decimal separators depend on the *creator's* regional settings, not on the file, so cross-locale CSVs mangle on open — the sourced guidance is to import via Power Query / From Text-CSV with explicit separator and decimal settings. Whether a given Vietnamese learner's machine expects commas or semicolons depends on their own regional settings — which…

nodes.label: 8.5 Localized example bank (summary)
nodes.text: 8.5 Localized example bank (summary) All examples are original designs — invented businesses, invented data, real Vietnam structures. Never a real company's data, a copied tutorial dataset, or a classic toy dataset. Design rules for every localized example: [Recommendation] - Money in VND, written the Vietnamese way in raw data and formatted cleanly in outputs, at realistic Vietnam scale (a single e-commerce order in the hundreds of thousands of VND; monthly store revenue in the hundreds of millions), so learners build magnitude intuition in VND rather than converting from dollars. - Names, addresses, and administrative units are Vietnamese: provinces / cities, districts, wards; phone numbers in local format as *text* (leading zero preserved — a data-type lesson in itself). - Calendars include Tet spikes, the local holidays, and the major platform sale days that dominate e-commerce data. Starter bank (one per domain, expandable): an Excel provincial sales workbook for a beverage distributor (inconsistent province spellings, conditional totals by region, a PivotTable of Tet vs. non-Tet months); an Excel/Sheets coffee-shop chain daily revenue sheet (payment mix, percent stored as text, average vs. median under weekend skew, an outlier day from an extra zero in VND); a SQL e-commerce orders set for a fictional marketplace seller (canceled-order filtering with Vietnamese status values, joins to products, grouping by province and month, funnel counts, repeat-purchase analysis — w…

nodes.label: 8.6 /vi/ build checklist (lesson-level)
nodes.text: 8.6 /vi/ build checklist (lesson-level) 1. One glossary source of truth implementing Section 8.2, with bucket tags; lessons reference it, never duplicate definitions. 2. Lesson template slots for /vi/ only, per Section 8.3: terms preview box, format callout box, "say it at work" line, English search phrases, error-reading drill where relevant. 3. Paired-dataset pipeline: every exercise dataset exists in an EN-context and a VI-context version with identical structure, traps, and answer shapes. 4. A single messy-Vietnamese-text dataset family reused across the Excel / SQL / Python cleaning units, including đ, stacked-diacritic, and no-diacritic cases. 5. Formula publication standard: English names, comma separators, standing separator callout on /vi/ pages. No translated formula variants anywhere. 6. Checkpoint bank extended with mapping items (term → meaning, VN request → EN operation, EN error → fix) for /vi/ only. 7. Date / number sanity-check exercises (day ≤ 12 swap detection, thousand-separator parsing, stored-value vs. display checks) placed in the Excel block and recalled in SQL and Python. ---

nodes.label: 9. Anti-patterns to avoid
nodes.text: 9. Anti-patterns to avoid Each anti-pattern names the failure, its basis in the research record, and the template rule that prevents it. 1. Tutorial hell / the illusion of competence. The learner finishes course after course and freezes at a blank file, because the instructor made every decision. [Sourced — pedagogy research: the most consistently described failure pattern across learner discussions] *Prevention:* template Sections 5–6 (fading, then a blank-start task as the lesson's real test) and the Section 5.2 rule that passing requires unaided production on unseen data. 2. Fill-in-the-blank as the terminal exercise. Supplying most of the solution and asking for the last fragment produces fast, pleasant progress and learners who cannot start from nothing. [Sourced — pedagogy research] *Prevention:* fill-in formats are permitted only inside the faded example (template Section 5), never as Section 6 or as a checkpoint item. 3. Clean-data-only teaching. Every exercise on tidy, correctly typed data, so the first messy file the learner meets is at work or in an interview. [Sourced — hiring-task research, rated a critical gap there] *Prevention:* one deliberate flaw in every blank-start task; repair rungs in the Excel, Python, and DE/ML ladders. 4. The given-metric shortcut. Exercises that always state the metric, the denominator, and the output shape, so the learner practices arithmetic while hiring tests definition. [Sourced — hiring-task research, rated critical] *Preventio…

nodes.label: 1. What the audit found — scores and the two poles
nodes.text: 1. What the audit found — scores and the two poles The audit scored seven platforms on four dimensions (1–5): beginner clarity (can a total beginner find the right starting point fast), syllabus transparency (how much of the actual content is visible before committing), visual teaching aids (diagrams, interactives, and worked visuals as teaching tools), and friction (5 = almost no friction; 1 = heavy walls and upsell pressure). Scores from the audit table, reproduced exactly: | Platform | Beginner clarity | Syllabus transparency | Visual teaching aids | Friction (5 = least) | |---|---|---|---|---| | DataCamp | 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 | | Coursera | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 | | freeCodeCamp | 4 | 5 | 3 | 5 | | Dataquest | 5 | 4 | 4 | 4 | | Codecademy | 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 | | Kaggle Learn | 3 | 3 | 4 | 5 | | roadmap.sh | 3 | 5 | 5 | 5 | Two poles define the open position: - The clarity benchmark: Dataquest. The clearest beginner information architecture among the paid platforms (beginner clarity 5, the audit's only 5 on that dimension). Its homepage separates Career paths from Skill paths and labels each path card with exactly the metadata a beginner needs to choose — skill tags, course count, project count, realistic duration, enrolled-learner count, and honest sorting labels such as "Best for Beginners" — with the Data Analyst path explicitly tagged best for beginners. Its free-trial terms are the most honestly stated in the audit ("No credit card required," stated in the FAQ and again at the footer)…

nodes.label: 11. Design-review checklist
nodes.text: 11. Design-review checklist A page or component ships only when every line below passes. [Recommendation] Clarity - [ ] A first-time visitor can name the right starting point from the homepage without clicking (path/stage cards carry skills, counts, durations, and a beginner tag). - [ ] The page states its prerequisites explicitly, including "none" where true. - [ ] Every time estimate carries its pace assumption; every outcome or demand figure carries its source and date. - [ ] The full syllabus is reachable in one click and readable without any account; lesson names, counts, and durations are published together. - [ ] The page carries a last-updated date. No dark patterns - [ ] Nothing on the page gates content behind signup, trial, or payment — and the page says the content is free where an incumbent would upsell. - [ ] No speed multiplier, deadline, or outcome claim appears without a source. - [ ] No streak, XP, or leaderboard mechanic punishes absence or rewards completion over recall. Visual teaching - [ ] Every hard concept on the page has exactly one canonical visual, shown before its syntax or formula, with labels on the visual itself. - [ ] The visual uses the shared grammar (tables, walls, buckets, chips) and holds its colors constant through the lesson; meaning is never carried by color alone. - [ ] The teaching data is small and rigged (a NULL, a tie, an outlier, or a duplicate where the distinction needs one). - [ ] Every interactive has step controls, a predic…

nodes.label: 2. Site patterns to adopt — copy in spirit
nodes.text: 2. Site patterns to adopt — copy in spirit Each pattern names its source platform and the page the audit opened (2026-11-15). "Copy in spirit" means: adopt the pattern's function, in Data From Zero's own design — never the platform's copy, artwork, or page text. 1. Path cards with decision metadata (Dataquest — homepage). Every path labeled with skills, course count, project count, realistic duration, and a plain-English tag ("Best for Beginners") on the homepage itself — a beginner can choose without clicking anything. Data From Zero applies this at two levels: the five tracks after the core, and the stages of the linear path itself, each card carrying the same metadata fields. 2. Full syllabus visible before commitment (freeCodeCamp — curriculum page; roadmap.sh — Data Analyst roadmap page). The complete ordered curriculum readable with no account; signing in — where it exists at all — saves progress and never unlocks content. On Data From Zero there is nothing to unlock: every lesson, exercise, and answer layer is public. This is the transparency standard the whole site is held to. 3. A whole-journey visual map (roadmap.sh — homepage and Data Analyst roadmap). One spatial chart showing the entire path at once — the natural centerpiece for a site whose premise is a roadmap. Adopted as *navigation*, with the audit's correction built in: the map is the table of contents, not the teaching. Every node opens a real lesson on this site (Section 4, item 7). 4. Course-page anatomy…
