nodes.label: 4. Patterns to beat / avoid
nodes.text: 4. Patterns to beat / avoid Each item names the pattern, the platform(s) the audit found it on (pages accessed 2026-11-15), and the counter-design. These are the site's anti-requirements: a design review that finds any of them on Data From Zero has found a defect. 1. Auto-subscription traps (Coursera). Enrolling in one course silently subscribing the learner to a whole paid certificate — admitted in that platform's own FAQ, and the audit's clearest dark pattern. *Counter-design:* there is nothing to subscribe to, and the site says so. No accounts gate content; no trial exists to convert. 2. Hidden pricing (DataCamp, Dataquest, Codecademy). Homepages that say "free" loudly and a price nowhere; one platform's full price discoverable only in page metadata, its projects, quizzes, and certificate revealed as paid in a bottom-of-page upsell block. *Counter-design:* a free site weaponizes this contrast — "free, all of it, forever" stated where rivals state nothing, including on the pages for the parts incumbents paywall (projects, checkpoints, review sets). 3. Catalog overload as a feature (Coursera, Codecademy, roadmap.sh). A five-figure course count marketed as value, four overlapping product types a beginner cannot distinguish, dozens of undifferentiated roadmap links — abundance while beginners drown. *Counter-design:* one curated linear path with progressive disclosure. nodes.label: 5. Visual teaching — the core lesson and the house sequence
nodes.text: 5. Visual teaching — the core lesson and the house sequence Confidence: High — the same pattern recurs across the visual explainers opened for the visual-teaching research (a visual introduction to probability and statistics; a visual introduction to machine learning in two parts; an interactive-article journal; two independent SQL join visualizers; a window-functions teaching guide; a Python step-through visualizer). All accessed 2026-11-15. The strongest visual teachers share one sequence, and it is the opposite of most incumbent courses: 1. Show the data moving first. The learner watches rows pair up, a distribution fill in, a split divide a scatterplot, or a variable change value — before any definition. 2. Name the mechanism in plain language while it is visible. The label lands on something the eye already tracked. 3. Only then show syntax or formula. Code and notation become a caption for a picture the learner already understands. 4. Let the learner change one thing and predict first. Drag a probability bar, edit a join key, move a split point, step one line forward — then compare the result to the prediction. House rule: no hard concept is introduced by syntax or formula alone. Every hard concept gets one canonical visual first. This exploits the dual-channel advantage the pedagogy research identifies — verbal and visual channels are separate and limited, so pairing a visual with concise text beats either alone — and it is the main antidote to math anxiety, because t…

nodes.label: 5.1 Cross-cutting techniques worth standardizing
nodes.text: 5.1 Cross-cutting techniques worth standardizing [Recommendation throughout — design synthesis from the sources opened; the per-technique evidence sits in the catalog, Section 6.] 1. Predict-before-reveal. Before any animation or stepper advances, ask what will happen ("Will this customer appear in a LEFT JOIN result?"). Reveal on click. This converts watching into retrieval practice, which the pedagogy research ranks among the highest-evidence methods available to a static site. 2. One shared visual grammar. Tables always look like tables, partitions always use the same wall style, groups always use the same buckets, a filter always uses the same chip style — across Excel, SQL, Python, and statistics. Recognition transfers; relearning a new diagram language per stage does not. 3. Color with a job, never decoration. One color per table, per class, per partition, held constant through a whole lesson and stated in a legend. Color is how the eye tracks identity through a transformation; changing it mid-lesson breaks the tracking the visual exists to provide. Never encode meaning in color alone — pair it with labels or patterns, for color-vision accessibility. 4. Small, rigged data. Every teaching dataset is tiny and deliberately loaded: a NULL key, a tie, an outlier, a duplicate — each odd row exists to make exactly one distinction visible. Realistic messy data belongs in projects; canonical visuals need data designed like a demonstration, not sampled like a dataset. 5. Step co…

nodes.label: 6. Technique catalog — mapped to the hard concepts
nodes.text: 6. Technique catalog — mapped to the hard concepts Build-cost key: Static SVG = one hand-authored or generated vector diagram, no JavaScript required. CSS = layout, highlighting, or transition in styles alone. Interactive JS = a small client-side component; vanilla JavaScript or a tiny framework island, no server, no account. Confidence is High where the technique is grounded in an opened exemplar, Medium where it is a transfer of a proven pattern to a new domain — and is labeled as such.

nodes.label: 7. What incumbents do NOT do visually — the ten gaps
nodes.text: 7. What incumbents do NOT do visually — the ten gaps Confidence: High — taken directly from the Wave 1 UI/UX audit and pedagogy research; no new claims about incumbents are added here. Scores below use the corrected grouping from the verification wave: DataCamp, Dataquest, Codecademy, and Kaggle Learn scored 4 for visual teaching aids; Coursera scored 2; freeCodeCamp scored 3; roadmap.sh scored 5 *for its map only*. Even the 4s credit screenshots, exercise imagery, and notebook formats more than concept diagrams. 1. Video-first passivity at the largest incumbent. Coursera's core medium is the lecture video, and its public pages show almost no interactive or diagrammatic teaching aids. A learner watches a join; they never watch rows pair up. 2. A map that teaches nothing. roadmap.sh's node chart states what to learn and in what order while teaching none of it. Every node is a doorway to external resources, not a lesson. 3. A menu with no path and no visuals of the journey. Kaggle Learn lists strong free micro-courses with no sequence, no prerequisites, and no visual model of how the pieces connect. 4. Text-wall transparency. freeCodeCamp exposes its full curriculum with no durations, no difficulty signals, and no visual hierarchy — openness without design. Nothing shows a beginner what a concept looks like before they commit to it. 5. Text-only process teaching. Dataquest's no-video, write-real-code model is pedagogically strong, but its own reviews note that learners who nee…

nodes.label: 8. Time-to-skill — the UX contribution
nodes.text: 8. Time-to-skill — the UX contribution Time-to-skill is one of the four tests the project is judged on, and the site's design — not only the curriculum's order — decides much of it. The mechanisms below are [Recommendation], each tied to an audit finding or a pedagogy finding; no speed multiplier is claimed anywhere (Section 4, item 6). - Zero setup, zero wall between arrival and first result. The audit's friction leaders are free and wall-less; every wall an incumbent adds (account before content, trial before syllabus, enterprise pitch before path cards) is time spent not learning. Data From Zero's first lesson starts on the page the beginner lands on, in the browser, with the dataset already there. - Decision time removed, not learning time. Path cards with decision metadata (Section 2, pattern 1), one linear order (no catalog search), and an always-visible "what next" convert the hours incumbents spend learners on *choosing* into hours spent *doing*. Choice overload is the largest incumbent's defining information-architecture problem in the audit; a single path is the fix. - Concepts arrive pre-understood. The visual-first sequence (Section 5) front-loads intuition so syntax is learned as a caption for a known picture, instead of being decoded and conceptualized simultaneously. The pedagogy research's dual-channel finding is the basis: two channels used well carry more than one channel used twice. - No re-learning of diagram languages. One shared visual grammar across st…

nodes.label: 9. Static-site performance and mobile constraints
nodes.text: 9. Static-site performance and mobile constraints Confidence: Medium-High — engineering guidance for the static stack named in the project plan (one site, Learn + Reference spaces). Everything in this section is [Recommendation]: design targets for Data From Zero, not measured facts about any external site. Accessibility items that originate in the visual-teaching research (reduced motion, color-alone encoding, static fallbacks) are build rules, not audit findings — no incumbent was scored on accessibility in the audit.

nodes.label: 9.1 Budget rules
nodes.text: 9.1 Budget rules - Static first. Every visual ships as static SVG or CSS by default. JavaScript is added only where manipulation is the teaching mechanism (sliders, steppers, editable tables, small simulations). A page with no interactive concept ships no component JavaScript. - Island discipline. Each interactive visual is an isolated island that loads only on its own lesson page, hydrates lazily when it approaches the viewport, and never blocks the text — which must be fully readable before hydration. - No heavy animation libraries for simple work. CSS transitions and native scroll/intersection APIs cover steppers, highlights, and reveal effects. Reserve any animation library for a proven need on a flagship visual, loaded only on that page. Load animation code after the page is visible and initialize each section only when the reader scrolls near it. - Simulation caps. In-browser simulations (coin flips, sampling, tree growth) run on dozens to hundreds of points, precomputed where the sequence is fixed. Nothing animates thousands of DOM nodes; if a visual ever needs that scale, it belongs on a canvas element with a static SVG fallback, and that decision needs an explicit reason. - Fonts and images. Visuals are SVG and HTML, not raster screenshots, so they stay sharp, small, translatable, and theme-able. Do not ship a video file where a scrubbable SVG sequence teaches the same point. - Two spaces, one component library. Learn (spacious) and Reference (dense) render the same…

nodes.label: 9.2 Mobile rules
nodes.text: 9.2 Mobile rules - Design the visual for a narrow screen first. The audit flags roadmap.sh's dense node chart as inherently hard on a phone; Data From Zero's visuals must not repeat that. Tables in a visual keep at most a handful of columns; wide tables become stacked card pairs on small screens rather than shrinking to unreadable type. The roadmap map itself, on mobile, renders as the ordered stage list with the same metadata as the cards — the spatial chart is a desktop enhancement, never the only navigation. - Scrollytelling collapses vertically. The desktop pattern (text beside a pinned visual) becomes, on mobile, alternating text and visual blocks in one column, with the visual sticky only where it remains fully visible without covering the text. - Touch targets and controls. Steppers, sliders, and join-type switchers need large, thumb-reachable controls, and every drag interaction needs a tap/step alternative. Dragging a distribution bar or a regression line must also work as plus/minus steppers. - No hover-dependent teaching. Anything revealed on hover on desktop must be revealed on tap on mobile, and must never be the only place a definition or result appears. - Reduced motion and pausing. Respect the reader's reduced-motion preference: animations start paused or in their final state, autoplay is never the only mode, and every animation can be paused and stepped manually. This is an accessibility requirement, not a preference toggle. - Offline and low-bandwidth reali…

nodes.label: 9.3 Risks to avoid
nodes.text: 9.3 Risks to avoid - Animation as decoration. Movement that does not encode a change in the data teaches nothing and costs performance, battery, and attention. House test: if removing the motion loses no information, remove the motion. - Simulation sprawl. Each interactive is code that must be maintained, translated, and tested in two languages and two site spaces. Ten excellent, reused components beat forty one-off interactives. Build a small component library — table-pairing, table-stepper, distribution, scatterplot-and-line, state-tracer, bucket-grouping — and compose lessons from it. - Canvas-only or JS-only content. Content locked inside a canvas or available only after hydration is invisible to search, print, translation review, and screen readers. Every visual needs a text equivalent that states its conclusion in words. - Screenshot teaching assets. A screenshot of a real spreadsheet, editor, or product UI cannot be stepped, highlighted, localized, or re-themed, and it ages with the vendor's UI. Teaching visuals are drawn components (HTML/CSS/SVG), per Section 6.3's canonical-visual rule. ---

nodes.label: 1. Job-Market Demand: Excel and SQL at the Top, Python Next
nodes.text: 1. Job-Market Demand: Excel and SQL at the Top, Python Next

nodes.label: 1.1 The corrected headline
nodes.text: 1.1 The corrected headline SQL is #1 or #2 in every named sample opened in this research. Excel is also #1 or #2 in every named sample. Which one leads depends on the sample. Any stronger claim — in particular, that SQL leads in every sample — is false on the research's own evidence and must not be used. The clearest counterexample is also the most concrete sample: | Sample | What was counted | Excel | SQL | Python | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | AccioJob, 328 job descriptions | Mixed data roles: Data Analyst, Business Analyst, Data Engineer, Data Scientist | 81% (267 of 328) | 60% (197 of 328) | 41% | Excel first, SQL second. Power BI at 43% in the same sample. Not a pure analyst sample. | | 365 Data Science analysis, via Traecta | Data analyst postings | 54% | 73% | — | SQL first, Excel second in this sample. | | Statssy analysis | 141,529 LinkedIn postings, Jan 2024–Dec 2025, 12 regions | 68% | About 73% on average across regions; 81% for the US alone | — | SQL first on average, Excel close behind. Regional variation is large. | | 365 Data Science outlook, newer Glassdoor US sample | 1,355 Glassdoor US postings | 41.3% | Around half | — | Included to show figures move by year and source. Do not treat 54% or 73% as permanent constants. | Read together, named samples for Excel and SQL span roughly 41–81% of postings, depending on skill, sample, and year. That span is the honest form of the finding. A second-hand pair quoted from a podcast transcript is dropped from th…

nodes.label: 1.2 Python, BI tools, and surveys
nodes.text: 1.2 Python, BI tools, and surveys - Python in analyst postings: use 40–50% from named samples. The AccioJob sample puts Python at 41% of its 328 mixed-role descriptions. The Traecta transition guide describes Python as mentioned in approximately 40–50% of postings. A lower endpoint sometimes quoted for Python appears in no page opened during verification and is not used here. For analyst roles Python is third, behind Excel and SQL. For data scientist roles the order changes and Python moves first — which is why Python sits third in the shared path but carries much more weight inside the Data Scientist and ML/AI tracks. - BI tools: Power BI reaches 43% in the AccioJob sample; across the samples opened, BI tools (Power BI and Tableau together) sit roughly in the 20–43% range. The lesson is not a specific percentage. It is that a visible-output tool — a dashboard a manager can open — is a recurring hiring requirement, not an optional extra. - Survey corroboration, kept separate from postings: Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey, as quoted on an opened comparison page, puts SQL at 58.6% and Python at 57.9% usage among all respondents. That is developer usage, not analyst job postings, and the two measures should never be merged. HackerRank's 2025 Developer Skills Report, via the same transition-guide source, ranks SQL first by employer invite volume, with demand growth reported at 25.5% year over year. - AI mentions: One opened comparison cites Indeed Hiring Lab (September 20…

nodes.label: 1.3 What the demand evidence does and does not justify
nodes.text: 1.3 What the demand evidence does and does not justify The Excel → SQL → Python order stands, but on two legs, not one: 1. Market leg (corrected): Excel and SQL are effectively tied at the top of analyst demand, with order varying by sample; Python follows for analysts and leads for scientists. Starting with either Excel or SQL is market-defensible. 2. Learning-sequence leg: Excel is the fastest first win for the path's core audience — workers who already live in spreadsheets — because it builds on an existing mental model (tables, formulas, summaries) before introducing a query language and then a programming language. That pedagogical argument holds regardless of which of Excel or SQL tops a given sample. Do not cite a false unanimity to defend the order. The corrected #1-or-#2 formulation is strong enough. Salary context for the home market, from a Vietnamese career guide opened in the research: entry-level data analyst roles in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are listed at 10–16 million VND per month for fresher and junior positions. Against that income, annual subscriptions priced in the hundreds of US dollars are a structural barrier, not a minor inconvenience — a point that returns in Section 5. ---

nodes.label: 2. The Interview Layer: How Hiring Actually Tests
nodes.text: 2. The Interview Layer: How Hiring Actually Tests Hiring does not test topics in syllabus order. It tests judgment under ambiguity, on messy data, against a clock, out loud. Platforms mostly test recognition and reproduction on clean data, untimed and silently. Almost every gap below traces back to that difference. A curriculum that teaches the same beginner topics inside hiring-shaped tasks closes most of the gap without adding new topics.

nodes.label: 2.1 SQL interviews: ten patterns and a five-rung ladder
nodes.text: 2.1 SQL interviews: ten patterns and a five-rung ladder Four independent interview sources converge on the same structure. A typical data SQL interview hands the candidate a small schema and a business-flavored prompt, watches the query being written live or in a timed assessment, and scores reasoning as much as result: clarifying the definition, stating the output grain, handling ties, duplicates, and null values out loud, and writing readable structure with common table expressions instead of one nested block. PostgreSQL is the safe default dialect in the guidance opened, because interviews usually grade logic over dialect trivia and allow lookup leeway on date and time syntax. The ten pattern families (ordered by when they tend to appear in a loop): 1. Filtered retrieval — return or count rows meeting layered conditions, including conditions in another table, in text, or in time. 2. Aggregation and conditional aggregation — summarize by group; compute several metrics in one pass; turn conditions into metrics with conditional logic inside aggregates. 3. Joins, including negative and self-referential cases — combine tables without inflating counts; find rows with no match; compare rows within the same table (for example employees against managers). 4. Top-N and ranking per group — pick the best, nth, or top few rows inside each group, with an explicit tie policy. The choice among row-number, rank, and dense-rank behavior is the test. 5. Time comparison — rolling averages, l…

nodes.label: 2.2 Excel hiring tests: three formats, ten task types
nodes.text: 2.2 Excel hiring tests: three formats, ten task types There is no single standard Excel test. Employers use three formats: 1. Short multiple-choice screens — what a formula returns, which reference type survives copying, which feature solves a stated problem. Timed in minutes; tests recognition and speed. 2. Hands-on simulations — perform the task inside a spreadsheet-like environment; the system checks the resulting state. 3. Live or take-home workbook tasks — work through a real file, watched live or submitted, where the deliverable is a workbook another person can audit, reuse, and trust. A learner trained only to pick the right menu item is prepared for the first format and exposed in the other two. The ten task types: 1. Tidy and total a list — sort, filter, and total over the correct range, with live formulas rather than hand rearrangement. 2. Fix a broken sheet — find entry errors such as a date stored as text, correct them without breaking formatting, make the sheet print correctly. 3. Look values up across sheets — bring a price or attribute in by code, including codes that do not match, and handle the not-found case deliberately instead of leaving raw errors. 4. Summarize with a PivotTable and answer in words — build the pivot and state the finding. Classic trap: the pivot shows a count instead of a sum because the amount column is stored as text. 5. Clean a messy export — split combined fields, trim stray spaces, remove duplicates on the right key columns, keep th…

nodes.label: 2.3 Analytics case questions: six families
nodes.text: 2.3 Analytics case questions: six families The case round tests metric judgment, not calculation. Calculating the wrong thing correctly is scored as a failure. Prompts are intentionally ambiguous — terms such as active user, retention, and engagement are left undefined on purpose — and the expected first move is clarification, not code. 1. Define the metric — measure the success of a feature, product, or checkout page. Scored on starting from user and business goals, naming one primary metric plus guardrail metrics that must not degrade, and matching the metric to the goal. 2. Diagnose a movement — a metric dropped last week; what do you do? Scored on a fixed order: verify the signal is real (tracking change, outage, holiday, definition change), segment (platform, region, channel, device, new versus returning), locate the funnel step or driver, form a testable hypothesis, recommend a next step. 3. Design an experiment — test a new flow or feature. Scored on hypothesis, randomization unit, primary and guardrail metrics, sample-size and duration reasoning including covering a full weekly cycle, success criteria stated in advance, and pitfalls such as stopping early on a first significant result. 4. Judge a trade-off or read a result — engagement rose but revenue fell; ship it? Or: the experiment shows a lift; do you believe it? Scored on weighing short against long term, checking data and randomization before celebrating, and proposing an explicit decision rule. 5. Interpret g…

nodes.label: 2.4 The Python round and the take-home
nodes.text: 2.4 The Python round and the take-home For analyst and scientist roles, the Python round is largely the SQL patterns translated into pandas, performed live on a small dataset and judged on idiomatic vectorized code as well as correct output: selection and boolean masking; merge as the join, with relationship validation, origin indicators, and predicting the output row count before running — including row multiplication from duplicate keys on both sides; groupby as a system, including transform for group-level values broadcast back to rows (filling a missing value with its own group's mean rather than the global mean, which gives materially different results) and grouped ranking and lag (an ungrouped shift leaks the previous customer's last value into the next customer's first row); reshaping, where pivot refuses duplicate pairs and pivot-table aggregates them; share-of-total and top-N per group with an explicit tie policy; and cleaning, type awareness, and vectorization over row-wise loops. Engineering tracks add pipeline-shaped work: ingesting messy files and nested payloads, validating keys, snapshot diffing, and writing output a rerun cannot break. Take-homes cut across all four formats above and are a genre with learnable conventions: - Shape: a dataset plus business questions, completed asynchronously. Employers commonly state 2–5 hours of expected effort, with a return window of about 2–3 days; actual candidate time often runs longer. Deliverables vary across SQL, a no…

nodes.label: 2.5 The gap table, compressed
nodes.text: 2.5 The gap table, compressed Fifteen gaps were cataloged in the underlying research. The three critical ones are not advanced topics; they are beginner topics taught with the judgment layer stripped out: - Metric definition (critical): platforms give the metric in the exercise statement; hiring requires choosing, defining, and defending it before computing. - Ambiguity (critical): platform prompts are fully specified with one intended answer; hiring prompts are deliberately vague, and clarifying questions and stated assumptions are scored behavior. - Data cleanliness (critical): platforms supply clean, typed, deduplicated tables; hiring supplies duplicates, nulls, text-stored numbers, late events, and many-to-many joins that inflate totals — and spotting and handling them is the test. The remaining gaps, in brief: grain discipline; ties, nulls, and edge cases; narration out loud; time pressure; cross-tool translation (the same pattern demanded in SQL, Excel, and pandas); reading and repairing others' work; workbook and code craft; experiment literacy; statistics in words; the take-home genre itself; performance follow-ups; and dialect and version realism. The curriculum response is placement, not volume: a timed hiring simulation at the end of the Excel block, pattern-organized SQL with a grain-first ritual and definition-first retention lessons, pandas taught explicitly as a second representation of the SQL patterns, a dedicated cases module in the advanced core, and two f…

nodes.label: 3. Projects and Portfolio: Proof of Work, by Track
nodes.text: 3. Projects and Portfolio: Proof of Work, by Track

nodes.label: 3.1 The cross-track rule
nodes.text: 3.1 The cross-track rule Every track source states the same rule in some form: proof of work outweighs credentials, depth outweighs count, and a live or runnable artifact outweighs a description. A hiring manager may spend only about 30 seconds on an initial portfolio review, looking for immediate evidence the candidate can solve a real problem, explain their thinking, and show results that matter to stakeholders. The three screening pillars are technical competence, business acumen, and communication. The consensus count is 3–5 polished, well-documented projects, recurring independently across analyst, science, and platform sources. The one deliberate exception is Data Engineering, where the bar is 2–3 deep projects. For ML/AI Engineering, one portfolio guide reports a pattern of 4–6 deployed projects spanning retrieval, an agentic workflow, an MLOps or deployment project, and one fine-tune as consistently landing interviews. Counts are targets for depth, not quotas to fill with clones. GitHub hygiene is part of the evidence for every technical track: a small number of pinned, well-organized repositories with clear READMEs, meaningful commit history, and no clutter of tutorial repositories burying the real work. For engineering roles the profile is treated as due diligence — the resume is the pitch, the repository is the verification.

nodes.label: 3.2 What platforms assign, and why it is not enough
nodes.text: 3.2 What platforms assign, and why it is not enough Platform work falls into four patterns: - Short guided browser projects (DataCamp pattern): scoped tasks on pre-loaded data, from about 30 minutes to about 1 hour for guided SQL projects, with the task, dataset, and success check all supplied. Structural limit: the learner practices execution inside a known frame rather than framing a problem, and datasets that cannot be downloaded leave finished work trapped inside the platform. The platform's own portfolio guidance names the fix — add a business question, a table description or diagram, each query with output and a one-line finding, a limitations paragraph, and one change made beyond the brief — and advises that three projects with clear write-ups outweigh twelve that stop at the last query. - Longer guided projects on downloadable, messy data (Dataquest pattern): realistic scenarios on real, messy, downloadable datasets, commonly 4–8 hours for beginner projects, rebuildable locally and publishable with documentation. This pattern transfers; the 3–5 polished-project standard is stated here as well. - Certificate capstones (Coursera/IBM pattern): one integrative end project. The older science shape runs a full methodology loop once, on a supplied problem. The newer engineering shape additionally demands governance, operations planning, and an architecture narrative — much closer to what engineering hiring screens for. - Competition work (Kaggle pattern): nothing is assigne…

nodes.label: 3.3 Per-track hiring bars
nodes.text: 3.3 Per-track hiring bars Data Analyst. Screened for visible fluency — SQL first as the near-universal requirement, plus Excel or Sheets, one BI tool (Tableau or Power BI are the recurring pair), and increasingly Python — and for at least one full-cycle project: question, data, cleaning and querying, visualization, insight, recommendation. Minimum shape: at least one SQL project, one Python project, and one dashboard project, plus a published dashboard a non-technical reader can use and a README stating what was done, what data was used, and what was found. Visible messy-data work carries disproportionate weight, because cleaning is a large share of real analyst work and the skill most underrepresented in beginner portfolios. Weak framing loses: a title that reads like a manager's question beats a title that names a dataset. Data Engineer. Screened for 2–3 deep projects that mimic a real pipeline end to end — a real problem statement, realistic messy or multi-source data, and a multi-stage design from ingestion through transformation and storage to serving — over many shallow demos. Reviewers scan a recognizable stack (orchestration, distributed processing, transformation and modeling, a cloud warehouse, Git) for how tools were applied, not merely that they appear. Engineering quality is scored directly: modular code, a reproducibility file or container definition, error handling and logging, and thought about reruns, mid-pipeline failure, and duplicate prevention. Reliabili…

nodes.label: 3.4 The ten gaps between assigned and expected
nodes.text: 3.4 The ten gaps between assigned and expected 1. Problem framing — supplied versus self-chosen and scoped, with stakeholder and decision named. 2. Data realism — clean, single-source, sometimes non-downloadable versus messy, multi-source, self-collected, with documented cleaning. 3. Originality — the same project completed by every learner in a cohort versus work that does not look identical to hundreds of other applicants. 4. Deployment and operations — ends at a notebook or in-platform dashboard versus a live artifact with container, CI/CD, monitoring, or an incident plan. Critical for ML/AI; high for Data Engineering. 5. Engineering workflow — solo browser work versus Git history, branches and pull requests, tests, CI, and a reproducible environment. Critical for Analytics Engineering, Data Engineering, and ML/AI. 6. Testing and data quality — output matches the expected answer versus visible tests on keys and logic, quality checks, validation gates, and failure handling. 7. Evaluation and honesty — a single headline metric versus baseline, appropriate metric, validation design, error analysis, and a limitations paragraph. 8. Communication for decision-makers — code and charts as the deliverable versus a case-study narrative readable in about two minutes: summary, finding in business terms, recommendation, limitations. 9. Architecture and trade-offs — rarely required versus a diagram plus written reasoning about grain, layering, tool choice, and cost. 10. Domain coherenc…

nodes.label: 3.5 The capstone ladder for Data From Zero
nodes.text: 3.5 The capstone ladder for Data From Zero Design rules for all tracks: - Four rungs per track. Rung 1: guided core (supplied question and data). Rung 2: messy-data rebuild (same skill, self-sourced or deliberately dirty data). Rung 3: end-to-end build (full track workflow, with tests, evaluation, and documentation as appropriate). Rung 4: capstone (self-framed problem, deployed or published artifact, case-study write-up). Learners publish Rungs 2–4; Rung 1 is practice. - One portfolio packet at every published rung: public repository; README opening with a one-sentence business problem; architecture or workflow diagram where relevant; how-to-run instructions; results in business terms; a limitations paragraph; and a beyond-the-brief note stating what the learner chose or changed. - One domain thread per learner, picked early and carried through at least Rungs 3–4, so the finished portfolio reads as a coherent story for one industry's hiring managers. - Review like a hiring manager: a two-minute scan test first (can a reviewer state the problem, approach, and result from the README alone?), then a deep review against the track bar in Section 3.3. Data Analyst ladder. Rung 1: guided SQL and exploration — a supplied business question set on one dataset, then a Python exploration of a second. Rung 2: messy-data cleaning story — combine two inconsistent sources, document every cleaning decision, analyze the combined result. Rung 3: dashboard plus recommendation — an interactive…

nodes.label: 4.2 What the cross-certification matrix shows
nodes.text: 4.2 What the cross-certification matrix shows - No single certification covers the whole beginner-to-job path. Analyst credentials barely touch cloud engineering; engineering credentials barely touch storytelling, and the AWS engineering guide excludes drawing business conclusions outright. Following only one blueprint leaves a visible hole. - Cleaning, SQL, and modeling recur everywhere hands-on work is tested. Every hands-on certification in the map rewards profiling and fixing data, querying with SQL, and structuring data into tables with clear relationships. Those are safe universal bets for core curriculum time. - Security and governance grow with level; they do not start at zero. Beginner material frames ethics, privacy, and appropriate sharing; associate material adds access control and row-level security; professional material adds encryption keys, sovereignty, and federated governance. The topic should spiral, not appear once.

nodes.label: 4.3 Alignment recommendations
nodes.text: 4.3 Alignment recommendations 1. Anchor the Excel block to the MO-210 blueprint, then go one step past it. Use the five domains as the completeness checklist, weight practice the way the exam does (more time on workbooks, formatting, and ranges than on exotic formulas), and add PivotTables and lookups immediately after, flagged honestly as post-Associate, Expert-direction skills. A timed, live-in-Excel practical of about 50 minutes mirrors the credential's format without using any of its tasks — with the duration understood as per secondary guides, as noted above. 2. Make the single SQL block satisfy three blueprints at once. The same block can serve the Google certificate's query-to-clean-and-analyze workflow, DP-900's relational concepts (features, normalization, common statements and objects), and the Google Associate Data Practitioner's expectation of writing SQL in a warehouse to answer a business question. Add one relational-versus-non-relational decision lesson, and end the block with a warehouse-style exercise on a larger read-only dataset with a short written conclusion. 3. Position Python as the Google certificate now does — after spreadsheets and SQL. Python for analysis in notebooks, as a productivity upgrade on problems learners have already solved in Excel and SQL, with no cloud SDKs, pipeline frameworks, or model training in the first block. End the core path with one end-to-end case — question, preparation, cleaning, analysis, visualization, recommendation —…

nodes.text: 5. Positioning and Viral Lessons

nodes.label: 5.1 What incumbents promise, and who is left out
nodes.text: 5.1 What incumbents promise, and who is left out - DataCamp promises interactive in-browser coding from lesson one, a path for every goal, career tracks, and exam certifications. Its free tier is the first chapter of every course only. Use one dated price formulation everywhere: list price about $28 per month billed annually; the pricing page simultaneously promotes an $11 per month special price (read 2026-11-15). DataCamp's own pages state different catalog and track hour totals in different places, so no single total is presented in this package as the total. Instruction is in English; subtitles do not teach a learner to read an English error message or write an English query comment. - Coursera promises university and brand-name credentials and career outcomes. Its free mode is a preview without the credential, and its format is video-lecture-first — learners who need doing more than watching, and learners for whom the certificate is not the point, are underserved. - Dataquest promises learning without videos, code from lesson one, real datasets, and honest time estimates. Content is in English only, and it offers enrollment in a path rather than a map of everything. - freeCodeCamp is 100% free as a public charity, with courses, projects, and certifications. Its core curriculum is developer-first, its data science offering is one branch among many measured in years, and it offers no spreadsheet on-ramp for Office workers. - Codecademy promises interactive lessons, guided…

nodes.label: 5.2 What actually gets shared: seven mechanics
nodes.text: 5.2 What actually gets shared: seven mechanics 1. A picture of the whole journey. A static roadmap image is screenshot-able, printable, and forwardable in a way a course catalog never is. The developer-roadmap repository behind roadmap.sh showed about 372,000 stars on its page when opened for this research, and its README ships share badges for major social platforms — the project asks to be shared. The artifact that spreads is the map, not the lesson. 2. Free, ordered, and open — creators amplify it for you. A free ordered path is content other creators can make videos about. The OSSU data-science curriculum repository stands at about 22K stars (November 2026), and creator videos walking viewers through free curriculum repositories reliably field one dominant comment request: the link. (For scale, the companion OSSU computer-science repository stands at about 211K stars, November 2026 — counts are date-stamped approximations because live counters drift weekly.) Distribution of this kind cannot be bought; it is earned by being safely recommendable. 3. No account, no paywall, no upsell at the moment of need. Free practice resources earn their place in recommendation lists with the same reasoning: short explanation, exercise against a real database, instant feedback — and no signup ambush that would embarrass the person who recommended them. 4. A public commitment device with a named handle. The long-running 100-days-of-coding pattern has two rules — practice at least an hour…

nodes.label: 5.3 Five positioning moves incumbents cannot copy quickly
nodes.text: 5.3 Five positioning moves incumbents cannot copy quickly 1. Vietnamese-first, not subtitled. Build the path natively in Vietnamese — explanations and analogies in Vietnamese, job vocabulary kept in English — with the English edition as the parallel track. Incumbents cannot copy this quickly because their content factories are English-first pipelines whose non-English offer tops out at subtitles over English exercises, or English only outright. Retooling thousands of interactive exercises into native instruction is a rebuild, not a toggle, and a single home market that is too small to justify that rebuild at subscription price points is exactly the right size to be a focused site's home market. 2. The whole path free, with no account and no funnel, as a stated public good. Not a free tier: the entire Excel → SQL → Python → tracks path, drills and projects included, readable and usable without signup, under CC BY 4.0. Incumbents cannot copy this because their revenue is the paywall — a first-chapter free tier and a preview-without-credential free mode are deliberate sampling funnels, and matching everything-free would cannibalize the subscription base that funds them. The one large exception needed a charity model and a decade, and still offers no data-first, Excel-first path. 3. One committed order with deadlines and pass/fail checkpoints — an anti-catalog. Exactly one path, in one order, with week-sized stages and a you-may-proceed-when-you-can-do-this gate at each stage. M…

nodes.label: 5.4 Honest limits
nodes.text: 5.4 Honest limits Incumbent learner counts are the organizations' own homepage claims and are reported as claims, not audited figures. List prices rotate with promotions, which is why Section 5.1 fixes one dated formulation instead of quoting whichever price a given page happens to show. No search-trend data is claimed anywhere in this file: trend tooling could not be opened during the research, and job-market evidence was used instead — arguably the better signal for a careers-first site, but a trends pass remains an open follow-up. And the demand table in Section 1 should be rebuilt, not merely re-dated, at each curriculum cycle: its own rows show that shares move materially between samples only a year or two apart. ---

nodes.label: How the branches build on the core
nodes.text: How the branches build on the core - Data Analyst applies the core: SQL L4 patterns and pandas to scoped reporting, retention reading, a dashboard design and model lesson, a BI tool lesson, A/B readout, case practice, a take-home and a case study. - Data Engineer takes `python-notebook-to-script`, `sql-modify-data-transactions`, and the core cloud, warehouse and Git lessons to idempotent loads, quality checks, Airflow, backfills, Spark and a design-and-defend capstone. - Data Scientist takes the evaluation trio (framing, leakage, metrics) plus regression and tests, then algorithms, cross-validation, feature engineering, interpretation, forecasting and experiment analysis. - Analytics Engineer takes SQL CTEs and windows, Git review, and the two data-modeling lessons. Slowly changing dimensions and views are deferred here from the core and SQL on purpose. - ML Engineer takes the core evaluation trio and the AI literacy lesson. It also takes three DS lessons (see the cross-branch edges below). - Cross-branch rule. Branches may not depend on each other, with one whitelisted exception: ML Engineer lists three Data Scientist lessons (feature engineering, cross-validation, gradient boosting) as prerequisites, because a concept has one home URL. `validate.mjs` fails any other cross-branch edge.

nodes.label: How the map is built
nodes.text: How the map is built - One idea per lesson, one visual per lesson. Each lesson names its canonical static visual (`visual:`). Playbook steppers and sliders (03 §7) are written as static frame sequences, because lessons ship no JavaScript. - Order follows prerequisites (D25). The graph module reports no cycles and no order violations. No lesson depends on a later stage. Only the first Excel lesson has no prerequisite; the first lesson of each later stage depends on the stage before it. - Stage sizes. Excel 22, SQL 35 (D40), Python 27 (D45), core 36 (D49), branches 11 to 12. Six lessons are marked `[stretch]` (the Python environments lesson no longer is, D45): nothing on the main path depends on them, so they can be cut or deferred. Without them: 160 of 166 lessons.

nodes.label: Ordering logic per stage
nodes.text: Ordering logic per stage Excel (22). Grid and tidy layout, formulas, references, then types and locale before any aggregation (a PivotTable on text-stored numbers is the classic failure, so "numbers are not numbers until you check" comes before pivots). Then tables, logic, conditional totals, lookups, text and dates, error triage, and a cleaning workflow. PivotTables, charts and a one-screen report close the block. Two bridges point forward: `excel-sheets-query-bridge` (QUERY as a preview of SQL) and `excel-xlookup` (the spreadsheet rehearsal for joins). The AI lesson comes last because it is gated on formulas learned unaided. SQL (30), one complete block. Tables, keys and grain, then retrieval, filtering, NULL, types, CASE. Aggregation and GROUP BY come before joins, so every join lesson can verify its row count with COUNT. Joins run inner, left and anti, then fan-out as a critique lesson, then self and multi-table joins. Then subqueries, CTEs (the house style from there on) and set logic. Window functions come last in the query half, with the hiring patterns after them: top-N, LAG and LEAD, deduplication, funnels, cohorts, date spine. Design basics (constraints, writes and transactions, normalization, indexes) finish the block before Python starts. The AI lesson is last. Pattern families 1 to 10 of 05 §2.1 are all covered. Python (27). One bridge lesson answers the same cafe question in Sheets, SQL and Python. Seven language lessons follow, taught for reading and recogniti…

nodes.label: Owner decisions (2026-11-16, SPEC D29)
nodes.text: Owner decisions (2026-11-16, SPEC D29) The owner approved this map; slugs are now permanent (SPEC §3, §14). Answers to the questions the map raised: 1. Scale. All 161 lessons stay, the seven stretch lessons included. `v1.0.0` ships when the four core stages (102 lessons) are published; the five branches follow in 1.x releases. 2. SQL engine: DuckDB in Colab (`pip install duckdb`, reads CSV and Parquet directly). SQL lessons use DuckDB syntax and cite DuckDB docs; a callout notes where common warehouse SQL differs. The dbt lessons use dbt-duckdb. 3. BI tool: neutral. Dashboard lessons teach the principles, then give short parallel how-tos for Power BI Desktop and Looker Studio. Cloud, experiment tracker and LLM provider stay vendor-neutral until a lesson needs one. 4. Datasets: one English set, prices in US dollars with cents. Vietnamese pages reuse the same data. 5. Smaller choices. Projects and checkpoints stay in lesson notes (no new content type). ML Engineer keeps its three Data Scientist prerequisites. The LLM primer stays inside `excel-ai-draft-and-verify`. The RAG practice text is course-written and becomes a dataset only when the first RAG lesson is produced. Source URLs marked `verified: false` (including every DuckDB, Power BI and Looker Studio page) were not opened when the map was made; check each one when its lesson is produced.

nodes.label: Why some stages exceed 12 to 20 lessons
nodes.text: Why some stages exceed 12 to 20 lessons - SQL (30, 28 without stretch). 00 §1 makes SQL one block: no later "advanced SQL". The inventory has 260+ items and ten hiring pattern families. Merging lessons breaks one idea per lesson. Twenty-eight lessons at about 25 minutes is about 12 hours. - Python (27). Four jobs in one stage: language (8 with the first-notebook bridge), files and NumPy (2), pandas and charts (12), workflow, exit and automation (5). The 8 to 6 compression the issue states does not follow from its own list (9 lessons in the draft block, 8 in the new one); see `06-curriculum-map.yaml`. The APIs and AI lessons are prerequisites of later lessons, and `python-environments-and-pip` is a required late lesson, no longer a stretch lesson (issue #61 section 9). - Core (25). Six areas mandated by the brief, each needed by all five branches. Statistics alone is 11. - Excel (22, 20 without stretch). The Excel hiring task types (05 §2.2) need ten distinct skills, and Vietnamese locale traps add two.

nodes.label: Evidence
nodes.text: Evidence Method (identical for every page): Lighthouse, performance category only, mobile emulation with simulated throttling (the default mobile profile: Moto-class device, ~1.6 Mbps, 4× CPU slowdown), 3 runs per URL, median reported. Measured 2026-11-15/16 (America/Los_Angeles). The PageSpeed Insights API could not be used: its keyless daily quota was exhausted (HTTP 429 on repeated attempts across two days), so lab data was collected with a local Lighthouse run of the same version family and profile instead. Absolute values from a local run can differ from PageSpeed's servers (shared-machine CPU adds variance, which the 3-run median dampens); the comparison is valid because every page was measured the same way on the same machine. CrUX field data could not be collected for the same quota reason; the PageSpeed links below run live and show field data where it exists. JS before first paint is reported as render-blocking script transfer flagged by Lighthouse; every measured page scored 0 KB there (scripts are deferred/async/module across the set, including ours), so the JS column is total script transfer. | Site — page | Perf | LCP (s) | TBT (ms) | CLS | SI (s) | JS (KB) | Render-blocking JS (KB) | Requests | Total (KB) | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Data From Zero — home | 96 | 1.78 | 79 | 0.000 | 3.90 | 57 | 0 | 13 | 131 | | Data From Zero — lesson | 94 | 2.60 | 0 | 0.001 | 3.34 | 34 | 0 | 18 | 166 | | W3Schools — home | 31 | 6.18 | 3,340 | 0.000 |…

nodes.label: Method and verdict on the draft
nodes.text: Method and verdict on the draft All 11 draft milestones were verified against a primary source and an independent second source. None was weak enough to replace. Four needed wording or precision fixes: - VisiCalc (1979): the title "The first spreadsheet app" overclaims — spreadsheet ideas existed on mainframes (Mattessich 1961, LANPAR 1969). Supported claim: first spreadsheet *for personal computers*. Exact release date found: 1979-10-17. - pandas (2008): the card must say pandas *begins* in 2008. It was not released that year — McKinney's own account says the code stayed proprietary for about the first year and a half; it was open-sourced in 2009. (Wikipedia's infobox "release 11 Jan 2008" contradicts its own history section and the creator; do not use it.) - Python (1991): exact date confirmed from the creator's own timeline: 1991-02-20 (0.9.0, released to alt.sources). One source labels the February 1991 posting 0.9.1; the card follows the creator's account (0.9.0). Month and year are undisputed. - ChatGPT (2022): title tightened to "AI in a chat box". No user or growth numbers are used — none appear in OpenAI's announcement, and the figures quoted elsewhere are company or analyst claims. One slot was open (11 draft cards, slider holds 10–12). It goes to the 1804 Jacquard loom, the documented origin of the punched cards the slider's own title names. Three further verified candidates are listed as alternates, and six as considered and dropped, each with reasons.

nodes.text: Priority Medium - outdated but still correct, or a clear beginner-level gap

nodes.label: Recommended final list — 12 cards, in order
nodes.text: Recommended final list — 12 cards, in order

nodes.label: 1. 1804 — A loom reads punched cards
nodes.text: 1. 1804 — A loom reads punched cards - Date: 1804 (patent year; the attachment was introduced across 1804–05) - Line: Jacquard's loom weaves patterns stored as holes in interchangeable punched cards. - Why it matters: The cards were data a machine could read — hole or no hole — the same "store it where a machine can use it" idea behind every table and file on this path. - Primary source: Science and Industry Museum (Science Museum Group), "Programming patterns: the story of the Jacquard loom" — https://www.scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/jacquard-loom - Second source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Joseph-Marie Jacquard" — https://www.britannica.com/biography/Joseph-Marie-Jacquard - Confidence: high — a national museum group and Britannica agree on the inventor, the 1804 patent, the card mechanism, and the documented line from Jacquard's cards to Babbage and Hollerith. - Disputes: Jacquard demonstrated an improved drawloom in 1801, and some references date "the Jacquard mechanism" to 1801; 1804 is the patent year for the punched-card attachment. He was not the first to use punched cards (Falcon, 1728; Bouchon used perforated tape, 1725) — his contribution was a practical, widely adopted system, so the card makes no "first" claim.

nodes.label: 10. 2012 — A job gets a name
nodes.text: 10. 2012 — A job gets a name - Date: 2012-10 (October 2012 issue) - Line: Harvard Business Review names data scientist the sexiest job of the 21st century. - Why it matters: The data careers at the end of this roadmap became named, hirable jobs in the years around this article. - Primary source: Davenport & Patil, "Data Scientist: The Sexiest Job of the 21st Century", Harvard Business Review — https://hbr.org/2012/10/data-scientist-the-sexiest-job-of-the-21st-century - Second source: IEEE Spectrum, "Is Data Scientist the Sexiest Job of Our Time?", 2012-09-27 — https://spectrum.ieee.org/is-data-scientist-the-sexiest-job-of-our-time - Confidence: high — HBR's own page confirms the title, authors and October 2012 issue; IEEE Spectrum confirms independently. ("Sexiest job" is the article's own title, quoted — not an added claim.) - Disputes: The article popularized the title rather than inventing it: the article itself says "data scientist" was coined in 2008 by co-author D.J. Patil and Jeff Hammerbacher at LinkedIn and Facebook. Davenport has said in later interviews that "sexiest" was an editor's wording.

nodes.label: 11. 2017 — The Transformer
nodes.text: 11. 2017 — The Transformer - Date: 2017-06-12 (arXiv v1 submission) - Line: A paper, Attention Is All You Need, introduces the Transformer, the design behind today's AI models. - Why it matters: The AI assistants you can now use while learning are built on this design, and they run on data prepared with skills from this roadmap. - Primary source: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", arXiv:1706.03762 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 - Second source: NeurIPS 2017 proceedings, "Attention is All you Need" — https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Abstract.html - Confidence: high — arXiv's own submission history gives the exact date, and the NeurIPS proceedings confirm the 2017 conference publication. - Disputes: None on date or authorship. One nuance: attention mechanisms existed before this paper (Bahdanau et al., 2014); the paper's contribution was an architecture based solely on attention, so the line credits it with the Transformer design, not with inventing attention.

nodes.label: 12. 2022 — AI in a chat box
nodes.text: 12. 2022 — AI in a chat box - Date: 2022-11-30 - Line: OpenAI releases ChatGPT: a large language model anyone can talk to in a chat box. - Why it matters: AI tools like this now sit next to your spreadsheet and code editor, and judging their answers takes the data skills in this roadmap. - Primary source: OpenAI, "Introducing ChatGPT" (November 30, 2022) — https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/ - Second source: Simple English Wikipedia, "ChatGPT" — https://simple.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT - Confidence: high — OpenAI's own announcement and the encyclopedia agree on the launch date, the GPT-3.5 basis and the research-preview framing. - Disputes: None on the launch date. Neutral notes: ChatGPT was released as a research preview, not a finished product, and the GPT-3.5 series had finished training in early 2022 — 2022-11-30 is the public chat launch, not the date the model was built. Closing card (site copy, not a researched milestone): "Now — Your turn." The learner's own first spreadsheet, query and script continue the story; no source needed.

nodes.label: 2. 1890 — Punched cards count a country
nodes.text: 2. 1890 — Punched cards count a country - Date: 1890 (Census Day 1890-06-01; enumeration began June 2, as June 1 was a Sunday) - Line: Herman Hollerith's electric tabulators process the US Census. - Why it matters: Each card held one person's answers as holes in fixed positions — a row of data — the same record-and-aggregate idea behind a spreadsheet table or a SQL GROUP BY. - Primary source: US Census Bureau, "The Hollerith Machine" — https://www.census.gov/about/history/bureau-history/census-innovations/technology/hollerith-machine.html - Second source: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, "Hollerith Tabulating Machine" (object record) — https://www.si.edu/object/hollerith-tabulating-machine:nmah_694410 - Confidence: high — the agency that ran the census and a national museum's artifact record agree on the inventor, the technology, and its use in 1890. - Disputes: None on the core fact. "Electric" is the Census Bureau's own wording ("electric tabulating system"); the machines are also described as electromechanical, since clerks fed cards by hand. Hollerith's patent was issued in January 1889 — 1890 is the year of first census use, not of invention.

nodes.label: 3. 1970 — Data gets tables
nodes.text: 3. 1970 — Data gets tables - Date: 1970-06 (Communications of the ACM 13(6), June 1970, pp. 377–387) - Line: IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd proposes storing data in simple tables of rows and columns. - Why it matters: Every table you create, and every JOIN and GROUP BY you write in SQL, follows the relational model this paper defined. - Primary source: E. F. Codd, "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks", ACM Digital Library — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362384.362685 - Second source: Wikipedia, "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Relational_Model_of_Data_for_Large_Shared_Data_Banks - Confidence: high — the publisher's record and the encyclopedia agree on author, venue, volume, issue, pages and month. - Disputes: The 1970 paper revises Codd's IBM internal report RJ599 of August 19, 1969, which the ACM Turing bibliography calls his first relational-model paper; 1970 is "generally credited" as the seminal public debut. No source disputes the June 1970 publication itself.

nodes.label: 4. 1974 — SQL is born
nodes.text: 4. 1974 — SQL is born - Date: 1974-05 (Proc. ACM SIGFIDET Workshop 1974, pp. 249–264) - Line: At IBM, Chamberlin and Boyce describe SEQUEL, an English-like language for asking questions of tables. - Why it matters: The SELECT, FROM and WHERE clauses you type in your first SQL lesson descend directly from SEQUEL's keyword templates. - Primary source: Chamberlin & Boyce, "SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language", ACM Digital Library — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/800296.811515 - Second source: Wikipedia, "SQL" (History) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL - Confidence: high — the ACM proceedings record and the encyclopedia agree on authors, venue, year and month. - Disputes: Wikipedia's infobox says SQL "first appeared 1973" — design work began in 1973, after the earlier language SQUARE; the paper itself is May 1974. SEQUEL was shortened to SQL because "SEQUEL" was a trademark of the UK firm Hawker Siddeley Dynamics Engineering; Chamberlin later dated the rename to 1977. Context only: Oracle V2 (June 1979) is described as "one of the first commercially available implementations of SQL" — keep that wording hedged; IBM's System/38 also shipped in 1979.

nodes.label: 5. 1979 — The first personal-computer spreadsheet
nodes.text: 5. 1979 — The first personal-computer spreadsheet - Date: 1979-10-17 (production release, for the Apple II) - Line: VisiCalc turns a personal computer into a business tool. - Why it matters: The grid, cell references and formulas you use in Excel and Google Sheets today follow the model VisiCalc set. - Primary source: Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston (the creators), "VisiCalc: Information from its creators" — https://danbricklin.com/visicalc.htm - Second source: Wikipedia, "VisiCalc" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisiCalc - Confidence: high — the creators' own site and the encyclopedia agree on the product, platform and year; the exact day comes from co-creator Bob Frankston's account as cited by Wikipedia. - Disputes: VisiCalc was publicly shown on June 4, 1979, and a few copies sold that summer; October 17, 1979 is the production release. "First" needs its qualifier: computerized spreadsheet ideas existed earlier on mainframes (Mattessich 1961; LANPAR 1969), so the supported claim is first spreadsheet program for personal computers.

nodes.label: 6. 1985 — Excel arrives on the Macintosh
nodes.text: 6. 1985 — Excel arrives on the Macintosh - Date: 1985-09-30 - Line: Microsoft ships Excel 1.0 for the Macintosh. - Why it matters: Excel is the tool this roadmap starts from, and its basic layout and core functions still match that first Macintosh version. - Primary source: Microsoft (Signal), "Formulas, fandom and an AI-fueled future — Microsoft Excel celebrates 40 years" — https://news.microsoft.com/signal/articles/microsoft-excel-celebrates-40-years/ (confirms the 1985 launch; the exact day rests on the second source and wide independent agreement) - Second source: Wikipedia, "Microsoft Excel" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Excel - Confidence: high — Microsoft confirms the 1985 launch, and September 30, 1985 is consistent across the encyclopedia and multiple independent sources; no competing release date was found. - Disputes: Excel was publicly announced earlier, on May 2, 1985; September 30 is the on-sale date. Excel was not Microsoft's first spreadsheet — Multiplan came first, in 1982.

nodes.label: 7. 1991 — Python's first public release
nodes.text: 7. 1991 — Python's first public release - Date: 1991-02-20 - Line: Guido van Rossum publishes Python 0.9.0, the language's first public release. - Why it matters: Python is the language this roadmap's third stage teaches, and pandas, Jupyter and scikit-learn all build on it. - Primary source: Guido van Rossum, "A Brief Timeline of Python", in *The History of Python* (the creator's own timeline; full-text mirror) — https://github.com/eltonlaw/the-history-of-python/raw/refs/heads/master/the-history-of-python.pdf - Second source: Wikipedia, "History of Python" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Python - Confidence: high — the exact day comes from the creator's own dated timeline, and the encyclopedia agrees on February 1991. - Disputes: Wikipedia's current text labels the code first published in February 1991 as version 0.9.1, while van Rossum's own timeline calls the February 20, 1991 alt.sources release 0.9.0. The card follows the creator's account; the month and year are not in dispute.

nodes.label: 8. 2006 — Hadoop brings big data open source
nodes.text: 8. 2006 — Hadoop brings big data open source - Date: 2006-04 (Apache changelog dates release 0.1.0 to 2006-04-02) - Line: Apache Hadoop 0.1.0 is released, spreading data work across many ordinary machines. - Why it matters: Hadoop's split-the-work idea still sits underneath the cloud data platforms beginners meet on the job. - Primary source: Apache Hadoop project, "Release 0.1.0 changelog" — https://hadoop.apache.org/docs/r3.4.0/hadoop-project-dist/hadoop-common/release/0.1.0/CHANGELOG.0.1.0.html - Second source: Wikipedia, "Apache Hadoop" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Hadoop - Confidence: high — the project's own release archive and the encyclopedia agree on April 2006, the origin in Nutch, and the creators (Doug Cutting and Mike Cafarella). - Disputes: Wikipedia's infobox dates 0.1.0 to April 1, 2006, one day before Apache's own changelog date of April 2. Month and year are safe; if an exact day is printed, use Apache's 2006-04-02.

nodes.label: 9. 2008 — pandas brings tables to Python
nodes.text: 9. 2008 — pandas brings tables to Python - Date: 2008 (development began at AQR; no exact date is sourced, and none should be printed) - Line: Wes McKinney starts building pandas at AQR, bringing spreadsheet-style tables to Python. - Why it matters: pandas is still the first tool most beginners reach for when cleaning and exploring a table in Python. - Primary source: "Wes McKinney", GitHub Readme Stories (the creator's own account) — https://github.com/readme/stories/wes-mckinney - Second source: Wikipedia, "Pandas (software)" (History) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandas_(software) - Confidence: high — the creator's account and the encyclopedia agree that work began at AQR in 2008 and that the public release came later (open-sourced 2009). - Disputes: Wikipedia's infobox lists an initial release of "11 January 2008", which conflicts with its own History section and with McKinney's account (proprietary for roughly the first year and a half). The card says pandas *begins* in 2008 and must never claim a 2008 release.

nodes.label: Suggested action
nodes.text: Suggested action Build the slider with the 12 cards above, plus the closing "Now — Your turn" card. If the design later allows a 13th card, add Google Spreadsheets (2006) between Hadoop and pandas — it is fully verified and needs no further research. Keep the dispute notes out of the card text; they are here so any future edit stays honest.

nodes.label: Type
nodes.text: Type Curriculum gap

nodes.label: 1. Framework and occupation codes used
nodes.text: 1. Framework and occupation codes used Framework: the quiz is *inspired by* the interest-matching approach of the O*NET Interest Profiler (National Center for O*NET Development, sponsored by the US Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration), which measures John Holland's six interest areas — Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional (RIASEC) — by asking people how much they would *like* doing single work activities, then matching the *shape* of the person's profile against each occupation's own interest profile. Our quiz borrows that idea (match on what a person enjoys, not on what they can already do) at a much smaller scale: 10 original questions, written for this site, mapped to four careers using O*NET occupation data (see §2 for why that is permitted). It is not the Interest Profiler, not a RIASEC instrument, and must never be presented as one. Occupation anchors. O*NET has no occupation titled "Data Analyst", "Data Engineer" or "ML/AI Engineer", so each quiz career is anchored to the closest real O*NET occupation(s). One correction to the original brief, verified on O*NET Online: Business Intelligence Analysts is 15-2051.01, under Data Scientists — not under 13-1161 (13-1161.01 is Search Marketing Strategists). | Quiz career | O*NET anchor(s) | Why | |---|---|---| | Data Analyst | Business Intelligence Analysts — 15-2051.01 (primary); Market Research Analysts and Marketing Specialists — 13-1161.00 (cross-check) | BI Analys…

nodes.label: 2. What we may use — licensing, checked against the official terms
nodes.text: 2. What we may use — licensing, checked against the official terms O*NET material sits under two different regimes, and the distinction decides how this quiz must be built: - The O*NET Database (occupation facts: tasks, work activities, work styles, interests) is CC BY 4.0: "You are free to copy or adapt the information from this database, as long as you: credit the O*NET 31.0 Database and the U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration as the original source, link to the license, and indicate where any changes were made to the original." The trait profiles in §3 are adapted from that database, so the quiz page must carry the prescribed credit (modified-information version): *"This page includes information from the O*NET 31.0 Database by the U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (USDOL/ETA). Used under the CC BY 4.0 license. O*NET® is a trademark of USDOL/ETA. Data From Zero has modified all or some of this information. USDOL/ETA has not approved, endorsed, or tested these modifications."* - The Interest Profiler itself (its items and scoring materials) is different: verbatim copying is allowed only under CC BY-ND 4.0 (no modified redistribution), and modifying or extending the tools requires the O*NET Tools Developer License — royalty-free, but it mandates the attribution notice above and a formal validation study before launch, conducted to the *Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing*. - Our approach stays clear…

nodes.label: 3. What distinguishes each career (the quiz may only separate careers on these)
nodes.text: 3. What distinguishes each career (the quiz may only separate careers on these) Scores are O*NET's 0–100 ratings from each occupation's own page (importance/impact/interest ratings — they compare occupations with each other; they are not percentages of workers).

nodes.label: Data Analyst — the business-facing explainer
nodes.text: Data Analyst — the business-facing explainer - Enterprising interest 57 (BI Analysts) and 75, leading the profile (Market Research Analysts), vs 12–34 for every non-analyst occupation in the set. - Business interest areas that appear nowhere else: Finance 58, Accounting 55, Business Initiatives 50 (BI Analysts); Marketing/Advertising 92 (Market Research Analysts). - Signature tasks: "Generate standard or custom reports summarizing business, financial, or economic data for review by executives, managers, clients, and other stakeholders"; maintain dashboards and BI tools. - BLS cross-check agrees: gather data, analyze it, convert findings into tables, graphs and reports, present to clients and management.

nodes.label: Data Engineer — the reliability builder
nodes.text: Data Engineer — the reliability builder - The only cluster where Conventional interest (85–94) matches or beats Investigative; Information Technology interest 93–95 paired with Mathematics/Statistics of only 37–50 — the inverse of the scientist profile. - Cautiousness 69–82 (Database Administrators' 82 is the set's highest) and Dependability 84–88; Innovation (41) and Tolerance for Ambiguity (44) bottom out here. - Signature tasks: develop database architectures; design for "scalability, security, performance, and reliability"; warehouse process models (sourcing, loading, transformation, extraction); security measures and user access levels. - BLS cross-check agrees: design and build storage systems, keep them efficient and error-free, secure and back up data, make data easy for users to reach.

nodes.label: Data Scientist — the open-question investigator
nodes.text: Data Scientist — the open-question investigator - Investigative interest 100 (Data Scientists) — the set's ceiling; Mathematics/Statistics specific interest 98 (Data Scientists) and 100 (Statisticians), vs 37–69 for all others. - Tolerance for Ambiguity 66 — the set's highest. Innovation 81 vs 41–68 in the engineer cluster. - Signature task found nowhere else: "Test, validate, and reformulate models to ensure accurate prediction of outcomes of interest." - BLS cross-check agrees: choose and clean data, build/test/update statistical and ML models, visualize findings, recommend actions to stakeholders.

nodes.label: ML/AI Engineer — the tool builder (medium confidence — see §1)
nodes.text: ML/AI Engineer — the tool builder (medium confidence — see §1) - Realistic interest 44 (Software Developers) vs 1–32 for all others; Engineering specific area 61 vs 13 or less everywhere else; "Thinking Creatively" ranked 4th among work activities (83) — no other occupation places it that high; Innovation 84, the set's highest. - Signature tasks: analyze user needs and software requirements; develop testing/validation procedures; design and modify software systems. - BLS cross-check agrees (Software Developers): design applications piece by piece, write and test code, maintain and document after release, work in teams. - The usable separator from Data Scientist is the output: models and analysis (scientist) vs working software systems that other people run (engineer).

nodes.label: Two clean axes the questions exploit
nodes.text: Two clean axes the questions exploit 1. Math depth: Mathematics/Statistics interest runs 98–100 (scientist) → 56–69 (analyst) → 37–50 (engineer) — the cleanest Analyst-vs-Scientist separator in the data. 2. Explaining vs building: "Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others" scores 87–95 for analyst and scientist occupations but only 62–63 for Database Architects and Administrators — it separates {Analyst, Scientist} from {Engineer}, though not Analyst from Scientist.

nodes.label: 4. Shared by all four — deliberately NOT used to separate careers
nodes.text: 4. Shared by all four — deliberately NOT used to separate careers Working with Computers, Analyzing Data or Information, Processing Information and Getting Information are top work activities in every anchor occupation (scores 73–99); Attention to Detail is the #1 work style in all eight occupations read, with Dependability and Intellectual Curiosity in every top set; Investigative + Conventional are the top two interest types in 7 of 8. These describe data work in general. The quiz asks nothing that merely measures them — and the result page says all four careers share them (see §7).

nodes.label: 5. Draft question set — 10 questions, original wording
nodes.text: 5. Draft question set — 10 questions, original wording Plain American English; no tool names, no jargon, nothing that needs technical knowledge; every option describes real work someone has to do, so no option is the obviously "smart" one. Weights: 2 = the career the option fits best, 1 = a close second. DA = Data Analyst, DE = Data Engineer, DS = Data Scientist, ML = ML/AI Engineer. Each question has exactly one 2-point option per career. Q1. You are helping a small shop make sense of a year of sales records. Which part would you most enjoy? - A. Putting the messy records in order, so the numbers can be trusted. — DE 2, DA 1 - B. Finding the story in the numbers and showing the owner what it means. — DA 2, DS 1 - C. Testing ideas about what drives sales, and checking whether they hold up. — DS 2, ML 1 - D. Building a small tool that answers the owner's questions automatically. — ML 2, DE 1 Q2. Which workday sounds better to you? - A. A clear checklist: the same reports run every morning, and they have to be right. — DE 2, DA 1 - B. An open question nobody has answered yet, with no instructions for how to start. — DS 2, ML 1 - C. A question from a manager in the morning, and a clear answer by the end of the day. — DA 2, DS 1 - D. A long project building something new that people will use every day. — ML 2, DE 1 Q3. At work, you would rather spend most of your time… - A. Talking with the people who need answers, and learning what they really need. — DA 2, DS 1 - B. Working on…

nodes.label: 6. Scoring and the result screen
nodes.text: 6. Scoring and the result screen Rule (simple enough to print on the page): each answer gives 2 points to the career it fits best and 1 point to a close second. Add up the points for each career. The highest total is your suggested direction; the second-highest is shown as your runner-up. Tie-breaking: if two careers tie on total points, the one with more 2-point answers wins. If they are still tied, show both as equal matches — for a suggestion tool, an honest tie is better than a fake coin flip. Result layout: - Headline: "Your suggested direction: Data Analyst" (career name filled in), labeled *suggestion*, never "match", "perfect" or "optimal". - One-sentence reason, generated from the winning career's theme (see §7), e.g. "because your answers kept choosing clear answers, explained to people." - Runner-up line: "Close second: Data Scientist — worth a look too." - The shared-core line (§7) and the disclaimer (§8) appear on every result. - Nothing is saved, sent or tracked; the quiz runs entirely in the browser. Say so on the start screen, not only at the end.

nodes.label: 7. Result copy — one sentence per career, plus the lines every result shows
nodes.text: 7. Result copy — one sentence per career, plus the lines every result shows - Data Analyst: "You like turning numbers into clear answers other people can act on — that is the daily work of a Data Analyst." - Data Engineer: "You like building the tidy, reliable systems that keep data flowing — that is the daily work of a Data Engineer." - Data Scientist: "You like open questions, patterns, and testing whether an idea really holds up — that is the daily work of a Data Scientist." - ML/AI Engineer: "You like building smart tools that other people can use — that is the daily work of an ML/AI Engineer." - Reason themes (used to build the "because…" line): Analyst — *clear answers, explained to people*; Engineer — *tidy, reliable systems that just work*; Scientist — *open questions and testing ideas*; ML/AI Engineer — *building tools people use*. - Shared-core line (every result): "All four careers start with the same core on this roadmap — Excel, then SQL, then Python — so this picks a direction, not a locked door. Switching later is normal, and most of what you learn carries over."

nodes.label: 8. Honesty and fairness — the checks this design passed, and the evidence behind them
nodes.text: 8. Honesty and fairness — the checks this design passed, and the evidence behind them - Suggestion, not assessment — and the research says it must be. A meta-analysis of 74 studies (Van Iddekinge et al., 2011) found a single interest scale predicts job performance at only about r = .10: interests say something real about what people *choose and persist at*, and very little about how well they will perform. The O*NET Center frames its own profiler the same way — a tool for "career counseling, exploration, and planning". The quiz therefore never uses the words test, assessment, score-based verdict, perfect or optimal, and the start screen says: *"This quiz suggests a direction based on what you enjoy. It is not a test, it measures no ability, and it saves nothing."* - No salary, demand or "best career" claims — none in the questions, none in the results, none in the intro. (Two of the four existing quizzes reviewed in §9 break this rule; see there.) - Known bias in interest inventories, and what we did about it. A meta-analysis of 47 inventories and 503,188 respondents (Su, Rounds & Armstrong, 2009) found a large average gender gap on the Things–People dimension (d = 0.93; Realistic d = 0.84, Social d = −0.68) — and, just as important, that effect sizes varied widely by inventory (0.08–0.79) and that item-writing choices "can substantially reduce sex differences": wording steers results. Mitigations in this draft: every career gets both people-facing and systems-facing options…

nodes.label: 9. Existing data-career quizzes — what they do well and badly (questions not copied)
nodes.text: 9. Existing data-career quizzes — what they do well and badly (questions not copied) 1.
