nodes.label: 1. What each source contributes — and its verified limits
nodes.text: 1. What each source contributes — and its verified limits CS 5200 (the academic spine). Syllabus arc: data modeling → relational design & normalization → realizing a schema → SQL retrieval → stored procedures & triggers → relational algebra & calculus → storage, query processing & indexing → concurrency, transactions & recovery → architectures → warehousing/OLAP. Lesson archive (55 lessons) adds the teaching assets: an ER/UML modeling set, Normalization, Relational Algebra, Query Processing, Indexing in SQLite, Transactions, and 17 SQL lessons including Subqueries/CTE (on a sample movie database), Joins, Views, Window Functions, Execution vs Syntax Order, plus two practice sets on a purpose-built practice database. This is the only source in the set that teaches design, theory and internals together. W3Schools (the practice floor). 46 tutorial lessons + 21 database lessons, all free, no account. Its "Try it Yourself" editor runs a real, writable, restorable database in the browser over a Northwind-style sample — the closest web equivalent of Excel's instant recalculation. Verified absences (checked 2026-11-17, including a 404 on the commonly cited normalization URL): no CTEs, no window functions, no transactions lesson, no subqueries lesson (approached only via EXISTS/ANY/ALL), no design/normalization, set operations stop at UNION/UNION ALL, indexes are one syntax page. Paid products sell structure and a certificate over the same content. Programiz (the zero-setup compiler).…

nodes.label: 3. The interleaved design — 7 movements
nodes.text: 3. The interleaved design — 7 movements One dataset story throughout: the café from the Excel drills, grown into a small chain (stores, staff, menu items, orders, order lines, customers, suppliers). Every lesson follows the same loop: Concept (one idea from the spine, in plain words) → Query (the concept as runnable SQL on the café data, in the same lesson) → Check (a known-answer self-check with the expected result published, plus one trap). Movements: 0. From a spreadsheet to a database. The café sheet they already know becomes tables. Why one wide sheet breaks (the same fact typed in many places, updated in one) told as a story; first CREATE TABLE + SELECT on the same data — the answers must match the Excel drills exactly (SUMIF West $1,025; capstone total $666.60). Spine: Need for Databases, Relational Model. Practice pattern: W3Schools-style instant editor. 1. Querying with a mental model. SELECT/WHERE/ORDER BY/LIMIT, then the lesson no tutorial has: execution order (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY) and relational algebra as pictures (filter = choose rows, project = choose columns). Spine: SELECT, Execution vs Syntax Order, Relational Algebra. Practice: Programiz compiler (SQLite) as the linked zero-setup sandbox; our own drills carry published expected outputs (the CS50 self-check device). 2. Aggregating is PivotTables. GROUP BY/HAVING/aggregates introduced as "the PivotTable you already know, written as text"; CASE as the written form of IF. Spine…

nodes.label: 4. How this differs from each competitor (the point of the design)
nodes.text: 4. How this differs from each competitor (the point of the design) 1. One dataset from Excel to SQL. Learners query data they already know from the Excel stage and can verify every answer against it. W3Schools/Programiz use a stranger's sample database; MindX's paid course skips Excel entirely; CS50 changes datasets every week. 2. Design and theory inside a beginner path. Normalization, execution order, algebra-as-pictures and query plans are graduate-course material (CS 5200) rewritten for beginners and taught through SQL only — no competitor in this study offers design + explanation + syntax in one free path. 3. Window functions and CTEs in the free core. Verified: absent at W3Schools, paywalled at Programiz, absent at CS50 SQL, blog-only at MindX. 4. Transactions and indexes as beginner lessons, with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN as a hands-on proof, not graduate trivia. 5. Every drill self-checks. Published expected results (adapted as a *practice pattern* from CS50) plus planted traps (the join trap already exists in our drills) — W3Schools/Programiz free tiers offer recall questions or unscored examples instead. 6. Citations instead of copies. Each lesson ends with named deep-dives (next section), so the site stays original while standing on named sources — and names MindX honestly as the local paid route for learners who want a classroom.

nodes.label: Summary
nodes.text: Summary ## Summary The SQL block is this site's core investment, so it should not be another syntax ladder. This report designs the block as an interleave: every concept from a graduate database course (CS 5200 Database Management Systems, Northeastern, Summer 2026 — the site owner's own course, archived by the team) is paired, inside the same lesson, with runnable query practice in the style of W3Schools and Programiz, self-checks in the style of Harvard's CS50 SQL, and an honest map of where MindX (the Vietnamese paid alternative) fits. Owner decision recorded 2026-11-17: SQL only — no R (CS 5200 used R as a delivery vehicle; it is stripped, the database knowledge stays). All practice data is self-created fiction (the café dataset from the Excel drills, extended), as with the rest of the site.

nodes.label: 1. What the learning science says (primary sources read 2026-11-17)
nodes.text: 1. What the learning science says (primary sources read 2026-11-17) Höffler & Leutner (2007), meta-analysis, *Learning and Instruction*. 26 studies, 76 comparisons: animation beats statics overall by d = 0.37 — but the moderators decide everything. *Representational* animations (showing the actual content) d = 0.40; *decorational* animations d = 0.05, not significant. By knowledge type: procedural-motor d = 1.06 (only 5 comparisons, confounded with realistic video), declarative d = 0.44, problem-solving d = 0.24 — the weakest category, and the one closest to writing queries. The study excluded interactive animations, so it says nothing in favor of passive loops specifically. Tversky, Morrison & Bétrancourt (2002), "Animation: Can it facilitate?", *IJHCS*. Reviewing the literature, animations routinely fail to beat *equivalent* statics; apparent wins trace to extra information or to interactivity and prediction bundled with the animation. Two principles: Congruence — the representation's structure must match the mental representation to be learned (motion only when change-over-time *is* the concept); Apprehension — the representation must be perceivable and comprehensible (animations are usually too fast and too complex). Their remedies: break the process into discrete steps, give the learner control, and ask for predictions. Mayer's multimedia program. The segmenting principle (learner-paced segments beat continuous presentation; independent meta-analytic estimates: retentio…

nodes.label: 3. The pattern across the market
nodes.text: 3. The pattern across the market 1. Every animation found is a passive, looping GIF. None can be paused at a frame, stepped, or scrubbed — exactly the format the science rates weakest (transient, system-paced, apprehension risk). DataSchool's GIFs are the best teaching animations in the set, and even they leave control behind. 2. All genuine learner control comes from running queries, not from visuals: Select Star's and SQLBolt's in-browser execution, DataSchool's SQLBox, Evans' Playground. Visuals explain; execution confirms. 3. The advanced end is empty. CTEs are taught visually by exactly one site (DataLemur, for interview candidates, in PostgreSQL-interview framing); recursive CTEs are taught by none. Window functions — the one concept where motion genuinely matches the concept (Congruence) — get a real treatment only from DataSchool's GIFs and DataLemur's narration. 4. Nobody combines the pieces: stepped statics + prediction prompts + a runnable query on the same tables + a permanent record of all steps. That combination is what the evidence supports, and it is unoccupied.

nodes.label: 4. Design rules for Data From Zero
nodes.text: 4. Design rules for Data From Zero Defaults for every SQL lesson visual (and reusable beyond SQL): 1. Stepped statics are the default unit. Each concept is a short sequence of static table frames — input → one change → next state → output — that the learner advances by click/tap (segmenting; apprehension). One change per frame, never two. 2. All steps stay on the page. A persistent strip of the frames (or a step rail) means no state ever vanishes — the direct counter to the transient information effect, and free re-inspection while answering the check question. 3. Predict before reveal. Before the step that shows a result, ask which rows survive / what the next value is (Tversky; Hundhausen). The check questions in issue #52's design slot in here naturally. 4. Animation exists only as a stepper. Where motion is used, it is the same frames auto-advancing with pause and scrub controls, learner-started, never an autoplay loop. No decorative motion anywhere (coherence; decorational d = 0.05). 5. Consistent visual grammar. Borrow the zine grammar (not the hand-drawn style): input table → the clause in a callout → output table; one consistent color per SQL clause across every lesson (signaling); page/section titles that state the takeaway as a claim. 6. Every visual sits beside its runnable query on the same café tables, so the learner runs the exact transformation they just stepped through (Select Star / Playground pattern). 7. Mobile-first frames. Steps stack vertically and stay…

nodes.text: 5. Suggested action Adopt §4 as the visual standard for the /sql/ build in issue #52: stepped-static frame sequences with prediction prompts and a persistent step rail as the default component; a learner-controlled stepper variant reserved for window functions and recursive CTEs; clause color-coding and the input→query→output grammar across all lessons. nodes.label: Summary
nodes.text: Summary ## Summary This report answers two questions for the SQL block (see issue #52): (1) does the learning-science evidence favor animation or step-by-step static images for teaching concepts, and when; (2) how do five strong SQL teaching sites — DataSchool (Chartio), Select Star SQL, SQLBolt, Julia Evans' zine, DataLemur — actually illustrate GROUP BY, JOIN, window functions, CTEs and recursive CTEs. Verdict up front: for SQL — abstract, symbolic, discrete table transformations — the evidence and the market agree more than expected. Stepped statics under learner control are the right default; animation only earns its place as a pausable stepper for genuinely sequential processes (a sliding window frame, recursion iterations); and the single most valuable visual for CTEs and recursive CTEs does not exist anywhere in this survey — both are open ground.

nodes.label: 1. Verdict in one paragraph
nodes.text: 1. Verdict in one paragraph The draft's pandas spine is right: its core sequence (select/filter, groupby, merge, missing data, dates, text, reshape) matches the common core of all five syllabi, and its order (small pure-Python block, DataFrame early) matches Kaggle Learn and McKinney. Four fixes matter. First, the single most-taught pandas skill in the field — deriving new columns with `map` / `apply` / `assign` (5 of 5 syllabi) — has no lesson. Second, the draft loads only CSV and JSON, although its learners arrive from Excel and SQL: `read_excel` and `read_sql` are the two most natural bridge lessons in the stage (4 of 5 syllabi teach multi-source loading). Third, the pure-Python block is one lesson heavier than the evidence requires and can compress from eight lessons to six. Fourth, the stage has no end-to-end analysis artifact, which 3 of 5 syllabi include. The draft's three distinctive bets — merge *validation*, notebook-to-script, and ai-assisted-code — are taught by none of the five; §2 keeps all three, deliberately, with the project's own justification rather than borrowed authority. ---

nodes.label: 2. Recommended lesson list — keep, change, add, cut
nodes.text: 2. Recommended lesson list — keep, change, add, cut Tags: [Keep] unchanged · [Change] same lesson, named additions or a new frame · [Add] new · [Cut] removed as a standalone lesson. The list is in teaching order.

nodes.label: Charts, web data, workflow, exit
nodes.text: Charts, web data, workflow, exit 21. `charts-matplotlib` — [Add by split] pandas `.plot()` plus matplotlib: figure/axes, the five analyst chart types, titles and labels, subplots, `savefig` to PNG (§5 gives the evidence for matplotlib first). 22. `charts-seaborn` — [Add by split] Seaborn as the shortcut layer on top of matplotlib — one-line statistical charts and themes — closing with the Plotly awareness box (§5). The draft's single unnamed "charts" lesson was carrying what Dataquest spreads over three courses. 23. `apis-and-web-data` — [Change] Names both halves explicitly so the lesson cannot quietly become APIs only: calling an API (requests, JSON in, DataFrame out) and one HTML-table read (3 of 5 syllabi teach scraping/HTML parsing as a skill distinct from APIs). 24. `environments-and-pip` — [Keep] Taught by none of the five as a named lesson — because the hosted-notebook syllabi own the learner's environment and a self-hosted roadmap cannot. Scoped to one workflow: create an environment, install pandas, run a script. 25. `cafe-quarterly-pack` — [Add] The stage-exit capstone (§7): one full analysis — load, clean, join, group, reshape, chart, conclude — on the café chain data the learner already knows from the Excel and SQL stages. Taught by 3 of 5 syllabi in some form; missing from the draft, whose last lessons were all workflow. 26. `notebook-to-script` — [Keep] Taught by none of the five as a named lesson; kept because it converts the capstone into a rerunnable `.py`…

nodes.label: Cut list
nodes.text: Cut list - [Cut] `comprehensions` as a standalone lesson — folded into lesson 5; only the one-line form survives. - [Cut] Set algebra drills, `while` drills, row-by-row loop processing, hand-parsing CSV with `split(",")`, manual counting/sorting/min-max scans — each is replaced by a named pandas verb in §2; hand-parsing additionally teaches a habit (it breaks on quoted commas) that learners must later unlearn. - [Cut — confirmed out of scope] OOP design and classes, decorators, generators beyond recognition, async, packaging and publishing, web frameworks, type-system depth, testing beyond one assert, algorithm and data-structure implementation. The developer-course contrast is CS50P, whose syllabus runs to unit tests, regular expressions and classes — a different job. Statistics and modelling libraries (statsmodels, scikit-learn) are *not* cut from the roadmap: Dataquest and McKinney both introduce them, but Data From Zero's own sequencing places them in the advanced-core stage after Python, so the Python stage only points forward to them by name. ---

nodes.label: Files and NumPy
nodes.text: Files and NumPy 9. `files-and-tables` — [Change] Renamed from `files-csv-json` and extended: CSV and JSON stay, and `read_excel` plus one SQLite query via `read_sql` are added (Gap: 4 of 5 syllabi). This lesson also hosts the DuckDB demo (§5) and the encoding rules (§6, traps 2 and 6). 10. `numpy-vectorization` — [Keep] One drill lesson at exactly the scope of §4: arrays, dtype, vectorized arithmetic, boolean masks, `axis`, `np.where`, seeded `default_rng`. No linear algebra.

nodes.label: pandas core
nodes.text: pandas core 11. `dataframe-first-look` — [Change] Now explicitly carries the summary toolkit — shape, dtypes, `describe`, `value_counts`, `nunique`, spotting duplicates (3 of 5 syllabi teach a named summary lesson; the draft had it only by implication). 12. `pandas-select-and-filter` — [Change] Names `sort_values` explicitly (taught by Kaggle and McKinney, named nowhere in the draft) and drills boolean masks as "WHERE for columns". 13. `pandas-derived-columns` — [Add] Deriving columns with `assign`, `map`, `apply` and one lambda pattern — the SQL bridge is "a computed column in SELECT, applied to every row at once". The largest single gap in the draft: taught by 5 of 5 syllabi, named by no draft lesson. 14. `pandas-groupby-aggregate` — [Keep] Carries two traps from §3: groupby drops NaN keys by default, and `count()` is not `COUNT(*)`. 15. `pandas-merge-and-validate` — [Keep] Merging is mainstream (3 of 5), but validation as a named practice is taught by none of the five — a deliberate differentiator, kept and leaned into: `validate=` and `indicator=` become house rules (§3, traps 1 and 6). 16. `pandas-missing-data-and-types` — [Change] Names `drop_duplicates` explicitly (freeCodeCamp and McKinney both teach it; no draft lesson did) and carries the pyarrow footnote from §5 — a footnote, not a topic. 17. `pandas-dates-and-resample` — [Change] Adds date-range generation and `shift` — `shift` completes the SQL window bridge, being the pandas twin of `LAG` / `LEAD`; time zones s…

nodes.label: Pure Python — the minimum, compressed
nodes.text: Pure Python — the minimum, compressed 1. `first-notebook` — [Keep] The entry every syllabus shares; also the first exposure point for the environment trap (§6, trap 1). 2. `values-and-types` — [Keep] Types and conversion are the learner's first defence against dtype surprises later (§6, trap 4). 3. `strings` — [Keep] Plain-string methods transfer one-to-one to the pandas `.str` accessor; f-strings carry chart titles and findings text. 4. `conditionals` — [Keep] Taught explicitly as the bridge: a boolean mask is SQL's WHERE applied to a whole column. 5. `lists-and-loops` — [Change] Absorbs `comprehensions` (one-line form only) and a one-section tuples note (`df.shape` returns one); loops are reframed as "repeat over files and names", never over rows; `while` drops to recognition only. 6. `dicts-and-sets` — [Change] Dicts stay at full strength (rename, `map`/`replace` dicts, `agg` dicts, DataFrame-from-dict); sets shrink to a recognition sidebar — pandas verbs (`.unique()`, `.isin()`, `drop_duplicates()`) do the set work, and Kaggle's Python course omits sets entirely and still reaches pandas. 7. `functions-and-modules` — [Change] Split in two halves: *calling* literacy (positional and keyword arguments, reading a signature with `help()`) moves up beside lesson 2, because every pandas call depends on it; *defining* small functions stays here, ahead of `apply`. 8. `errors-and-debugging` — [Keep] Validated: McKinney and Dataquest are the two syllabi that teach error-reading to b…

nodes.label: 3. The SQL bridge — what transfers, and the traps that must be taught
nodes.text: 3. The SQL bridge — what transfers, and the traps that must be taught For clean data the translation is close to one-to-one, and pandas' own *Comparison with SQL* page is the anchor: `SELECT` columns → `df[[...]]`; a computed column → `assign(...)`; `WHERE` → a boolean mask (`&` / `|`, never `and` / `or`, each condition in parentheses); `IS NULL` → `isna()` / `notna()`; `GROUP BY` + `COUNT(*)` → `groupby(...).size()`; joins → `merge(..., how=...)` including `cross`; `DISTINCT` → `drop_duplicates()`; `ORDER BY` → `sort_values`; `LIMIT` → `head`; `UNION ALL` → `concat`, `UNION` → `concat` + `drop_duplicates`; window functions split into three pandas families — `rank(method="min")` is `RANK()`, `method="dense"` is `DENSE_RANK()`, `groupby(...).shift(1)` is `LAG`, `cumsum()` / `rolling()` / `expanding()` divide up `SUM() OVER (...)`. Two structural differences have no syntax twin: there is no `HAVING` (aggregate first, then filter the result — or `groupby.filter()` when the original rows are needed back), and there is no `WITH` (a CTE becomes a named intermediate DataFrame — [Recommendation] teach "one named DataFrame per CTE" as a style rule; it also makes each step printable and debuggable). Everything that breaks in practice breaks around missing values, duplicate keys and the index. These twelve traps are the taught content of the bridge; each is documented in the pandas user guide or API reference (§8): 1. Missing join keys match each other. In SQL, NULL keys never join; in…

nodes.label: 4. NumPy — one lesson for the analyst, the rest deferred
nodes.text: 4. NumPy — one lesson for the analyst, the rest deferred [Recommendation] The analyst minimum is one drill lesson, placed before the first DataFrame (where McKinney puts his Chapter 4 and where the draft already has it): creating arrays (`np.array`, `zeros`, `ones`, `arange`, `linspace`) and reading `.shape` / `.ndim` / `.dtype`; vectorized arithmetic and ufuncs with no loops; boolean masks and counting with `.sum()` on a boolean array — this *is* pandas boolean indexing seen one level down; reductions with `axis=`; `np.where` as the array form of `CASE WHEN`; broadcasting at recognition level (the two friendly cases and the error message, not the general rule); random with a seed the modern way — `rng = np.random.default_rng(42)` — explicitly *not* the legacy `np.random.seed(42)` pattern copied from older tutorials; sorting and `np.unique` at recognition level, since pandas covers both in daily work. The data-scientist layer is deferred in every named source and is deferred here: matrix product (`@` / `matmul`, and that `*` is element-wise), the `numpy.linalg` toolkit (`solve`, `lstsq`, `eig`, `svd`, `qr` — McKinney lists it as a reference table, not as analyst technique), distribution-level simulation, full broadcasting rules, fancy indexing and array internals. Placement evidence agrees three ways: McKinney teaches NumPy before pandas but closes the chapter at the matrix material; DataCamp's introductory NumPy course runs arrays → mathematics → transformations; and Kaggle…

nodes.label: 5. Newer tools and chart libraries
nodes.text: 5. Newer tools and chart libraries The demand evidence (named sample only). Five real data-analyst postings, opened 2026-11-18: Nordstrom (Data Analyst, Omnichannel Engagement), Shell (Data Science Analyst), an unnamed consumer-tech company via hirist.tech on Jooble (Data Analyst, Python/SQL), Cross Border Talents for a financial-services client (Data Analyst), and Lazard (Quantitative Data Analyst). Counts in this sample: Python 5 of 5 · pandas 5 of 5 · matplotlib 3 of 5 · seaborn 3 of 5 (always paired with matplotlib, never alone) · Plotly 1 of 5 (as Plotly Dash, a dashboard tool) · Polars 2 of 5 (never as a core requirement — once as an accepted alternative to pandas, once as "familiarity") · DuckDB 2 of 5 (same soft language) · pyarrow 0 of 5. Polars — awareness only [Recommendation]. A separate, multithreaded DataFrame library whose own comparison page sells it on performance over medium and large datasets — a problem beginners do not yet have — and whose expression syntax is a second DataFrame language to learn. One "where next" box; no drills, no parallel syntax. DuckDB — awareness plus one guided demo [Recommendation]. The exception, because this cohort has already paid for SQL: DuckDB's Python docs show `duckdb.sql(...)` querying pandas DataFrames and files directly (`SELECT ... FROM pandas_df`), so one worked example inside lesson 9 — one GROUP BY over a DataFrame and over the CSV itself, result back with `.df()` — buys the "SQL on anything" trick at near-zero new-…

nodes.text: 7. Stage exit and free proof points Exit artifact [Recommendation] — the Café Chain Quarterly Pack. Three files on the project's café chain data: the cleaned orders dataset (CSV), the notebook that produced it, and a one-page findings note whose every headline number traces to a notebook cell. The notebook must show the full analyst loop — read, inspect, clean (missing values, dtypes, dates, text), join orders to stores and products, group and reshape, chart. It proves transfer across all three tools on one dataset and is portfolio-ready as-is. Two companions: the same analysis re-delivered as a rerunnable `.py` script (lesson 26's real test — someone else reproduces the outputs without opening the notebook), and optionally a SQL↔pandas twin notebook — ten fixed café questions answered both ways, with a note wherever the two behaviours differ (§3 made personal). nodes.label: 9. Addendum (2026-11-18) — Learning environment: Colab, decided
nodes.text: 9. Addendum (2026-11-18) — Learning environment: Colab, decided Question added after delivery: when learning Python, do learners prefer Google Colab / their own setup, or the learning platform's own environment? Finding: no large survey asks this directly; the evidence is behavioural. (1) Every major interactive platform converged on a hosted in-platform runtime — Kaggle Learn (hosted notebooks), Dataquest and DataCamp (in-browser editors), Codecademy (in-browser) — with zero setup as the headline feature. (2) A documented university cohort (Hochegger, *Teaching Python to Biology Undergraduates*, 60 students, opened 2026-11-18) ran the progression in-page Pyodide → Colab → local development: browser-first removed setup friction, but only 5 of 60 students voluntarily moved to local development, and the instructor's corrective is to make local development mandatory and scheduled in the next iteration. (3) freeCodeCamp is the counterexample model — no in-page runtime; lessons plus Jupyter taught explicitly, projects in an external notebook environment. A small Peruvian Colab study (8 students) reported learners wanted to continue on Colab; sample too small to carry weight. Owner decision (2026-11-18): Google Colab is the Python stage's practice environment. This site is static and cannot host a runtime like Dataquest's; the SPEC's Milestone 4 Open-in-Colab buttons are the equivalent of in-platform practice, and they also pre-empt trap 1 in §6 (install/kernel confusion on day on…

nodes.label: Python for Data (Not Python for Developers) — Research Report
nodes.text: Python for Data (Not Python for Developers) — Research Report Purpose. A check of the draft Python stage (25 lessons) against the field, with the gaps filled, so the owner can decide keep / change / add / cut lesson by lesson. The stage sits third in the decided linear path — Excel → SQL (35 lessons) → Python → advanced core → four tracks (Data Analyst, Data Engineer, Data Scientist, ML/AI Engineer) — and its learners arrive knowing spreadsheets, SQL joins, GROUP BY, window functions and CTEs. Scope is the analyst's daily Python: notebooks, files and APIs, pandas, NumPy basics, charts, small functions, reading errors, one runnable script, environments and pip. Out of scope (confirmed in §7): object-oriented design, decorators, generators beyond recognition, async, packaging, web frameworks, testing frameworks, hand-implemented algorithms. Method. Five research lines, all sources opened 2026-11-18: (A) coverage — the draft compared against five respected syllabi (Kaggle Learn Python + Pandas, freeCodeCamp Data Analysis with Python, Dataquest Data Analyst in Python, McKinney's *Python for Data Analysis* 3rd ed., pandas official Getting Started tutorials); (B) the SQL↔pandas bridge, anchored in pandas' own documentation including its *Comparison with SQL* page; (C) newer tools and chart libraries, from official docs plus a named sample of five real job postings; (D) beginner pain points, from official documentation; (E) minimum Python, stage exit and proof points, from Kaggle L…

nodes.text: Suggested action Adopt the recommended list in the Evidence report (27 lessons + 2 awareness boxes): compress the pre-DataFrame block from 8 lessons to 6; add pandas-derived-columns; extend files-csv-json into files-and-tables (add read_excel, read_sql, one DuckDB demo); split charts into charts-matplotlib then charts-seaborn (Plotly awareness only); add the cafe-quarterly-pack capstone before notebook-to-script; keep ai-assisted-code, environments-and-pip, notebook-to-script and merge validation as deliberate differentiators. Teach the 12 SQL-bridge traps in the lessons named in the report. Build work is structural (lesson list, curriculum map, notebook skeletons in the Drive folder named in the Summary); lesson prose remains the owner's.

nodes.label: Summary
nodes.text: Summary The draft Python stage (25 lessons) was checked against five respected Python-for-data syllabi (Kaggle Learn, freeCodeCamp, Dataquest, McKinney's Python for Data Analysis 3rd ed., pandas Getting Started). Its pandas spine and order are right, but it misses the field's most-taught pandas skill (deriving columns with map/apply/assign, 5 of 5 syllabi), loads only CSV/JSON although its learners arrive from Excel and SQL, carries one pure-Python lesson too many, and has no end-to-end exit artifact. Twelve SQL-to-pandas behaviour traps are named for teaching. Separately, the stage's practice environment is decided: Google Colab, with lesson notebooks stored in the Drive folder "Data From Zero — Colab Notebooks" under the project account (folder: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1vWGvs3VEU14gYC_j-cLudnqJmBhYCj6Y).

nodes.label: 3. Visual and exercise ideas — described in words, ours to draw
nodes.text: 3. Visual and exercise ideas — described in words, ours to draw All visuals below are original designs for the café dataset, specified in words only. They follow the visual-teaching rules already adopted in issue #58: stepped statics as the default (learner-paced frames, every step stays on the page, predict-before-reveal), learner-controlled stepper animation only for window functions and recursive CTEs, no autoplay loops, no Venn diagrams for joins.

nodes.label: Exercise ideas
nodes.text: Exercise ideas 1. Predict the output (before any Run). Borrowed from Kaggle's opening move and generalised: every Learn-by-doing unit shows code and its *hidden* result; the learner commits to a prediction (in the notebook, a multiple-choice or typed guess) before the result is revealed. Our lesson shape already has the Predict slot — the finding is that it should carry marks, not just attention. 2. Inspect the mask. Before filtering, the learner states in plain words which rows will be True (or counts them). Checked against the printed mask. The exercise that makes finding 2 stick. 3. Predict the row count. Before every merge and concat, the learner writes the expected output row count and one reason. Checked against `.shape` after running. Converts the merge traps from surprises into tests. 4. Adversarial trap cases. Each trap in issue #61's list gets one exercise case designed so the naive answer is wrong: duplicate keys in a merge, a missing group key in a groupby, NFD-normalised names in a filter, `!=` keeping NaN rows. Directly answers the documented learntools false-pass failure. 5. Escalation pairs. Kaggle's pattern of a question and its harder twin (its 3a/3b expression-editing pair, with a 🌶 marker for the spicy variant): a base exercise, then the same task with one constraint added. Cheap to author, honest about difficulty. 6. Blank-cell rewrite. The anti-over-guidance exercise (finding 8): "produce this exact result again — the cell below is empty." Appears from…

nodes.label: Visuals
nodes.text: Visuals 1. The annotated café table. A small café orders table drawn as a grid; the column-name band shaded one colour, the row-label band a second, the data cells a third — the same three-region idea the field's best diagrams converge on, drawn on our data with our labels. Used in `dataframe-first-look`, reused silently in every later lesson's tables so the regions stay familiar. 2. The mask, in three frames. Frame 1: the café table. Frame 2: the same table with one extra column beside it holding True/False for a stated condition, the True rows tinted. Frame 3: only the tinted rows remain. The learner predicts frame 3's row count before revealing it. Used in `pandas-select-and-filter` and echoed in `conditionals`. 3. Split, apply, combine — three panels. Panel 1: the café orders table. Panel 2: the table separated into per-store piles, one pile shown with its sum being computed inside it. Panel 3: the piles' results stacked into a small summary table. A fourth, trap panel shows the pile whose key is missing, set aside with a question mark — its fate is the lesson's Predict question. Used in `pandas-groupby-aggregate`. 4. The merge flow. nodes.text: Summary The Python stage's structure is locked (issue #61); this research covers what #61 did not: HOW each of the 27 lessons should teach. Five research lines opened the actual lesson pages of Kaggle Learn, the pandas docs, DataCamp, Dataquest, Codecademy, freeCodeCamp, Google, W3Schools, Real Python, McKinney's book (open edition), CS50P, and Vietnamese sources (HowKTeam, MindX), plus named review sources for learner voice. Headlines: predict-first openings win but Kaggle assumes prior coding; the boolean mask must be printed alone before use; groupby has three working doors (value_counts, PivotTable, split-apply-combine); value-based checkers false-pass and break on out-of-order execution; priced hints are the most resented mechanic in reviews; the most repeated learner complaint everywhere is fill-in-the-blank over-guidance; the Excel/SQL bridge is the field's open lane, and the honest bridge pattern is "match, then diverge" (VLOOKUP is map(), not merge). The Vietnamese lane is empty: free Vietnamese Python is developer Python with no pandas, and every Vietnamese pandas course is paid. Full report in the Evidence field: 10 findings, a per-lesson table for all 27 lessons, and original visual/exercise designs described in words.

nodes.label: 3. The verification checklist (taught in lesson 2)
nodes.text: 3. The verification checklist (taught in lesson 2) Compiled from cluster F §3 — the eight checks that catch AI data errors, in the order a working data person runs them: 1. Predict before you run. Write the expected shape, grain and a few expected values *before* executing AI-written code; a mismatch is a finding, not a surprise. 2. Judge the plan first. Join keys, join type, expected cardinality, output grain — approved on paper before code exists (finding 2). 3. Run it on the trap table. A tiny known-answer table with duplicate keys, null join columns and boundary dates; AI code must reproduce the known answers exactly. 4. Reconcile independently. One headline total computed a second way (different tool or different path — SQL vs pandas) must match. 5. Check the silent places. Row counts before/after every filter and join; null counts in key columns; fan-out shows up as row growth. 6. Verify every API call exists. Function names and arguments checked against the library's own docs — hallucinated functions are a named failure mode, not bad luck. 7. Read the code you keep. Explain-back: any line the learner cannot explain gets rewritten by the learner or removed. 8. Ask the AI to attack its own answer. A second prompt for edge cases and counterexamples — engaged mode applied to verification itself. ---

nodes.text: Where DSA Belongs: Research Report Purpose. Data structures and algorithms (DSA) is the hardest item left unplaced in the roadmap: genuinely difficult, and famously hungry for practice. This report answers three questions: what do the four roles (DA, DE, DS, MLE) actually need — split into *on the job* versus *in interviews*; does the curriculum package's earlier cut (§8.2: no hand-implemented sorting/data structures, no formal Big-O in the core path) survive the evidence; and where, structurally, should DSA live in a roadmap of static lessons, Colab notebooks and one café dataset? Method. Visualization and storytelling is DA's joint-most-demanded skill in postings (10/10, tied with SQL; 0/12 for both DE and MLE) and a standalone named skill in DDaT and SFIA 9 (VISL, whose update adds "narratives and storytelling around data") — and the draft has no axis for it. Without it, the DA profile is missing its peak. 2. No original score moves by more than one point. The draft's judgment was broadly sound. The moves: DS ML and modeling 4→5 (postings 11/11 — definitional); MLE Statistics 3→4 and MLE Pipelines 3→4 (on the merged axis, §3); DA Statistics 2→3; DS Experiments 4→3; DA/DS Pipelines 1→2 each. Everything else stands. 3. "Cloud/infrastructure" should not be its own axis — merge it into Pipelines. Postings bundle the two (DE: pipelines 12/12, cloud 11/12, usually in the same sentence); as separate axes they would trace near-identical shapes for DE. The merged axis reads "Pipelines, platforms and cloud." 4. "Domain knowledge" should not be an axis either. Explicit entry demand is near-flat (postings: DA 1/10, DE 2/12, DS 3/11, MLE 0/12; would-be scores 3/1/2/1) because at entry it is an employer-context layer — which industry hires you — not a skill a track teaches. nodes.label: 5. What career switchers misjudge (Q4) — the page's warnings
nodes.text: 5. What career switchers misjudge (Q4) — the page's warnings Full sourced list: Cluster L comment. The strongest warning per role, plus the cross-role one: - All roles — the headline skill is a minority of the week. Data preparation is the plurality activity in every survey (§1, finding 9); communication is the second surprise (Anaconda 2022: reporting/presentation 16.20% + visualization 12.99% ≈ 29% of time). And titles mislead: role content varies sharply by employer (Built In notes "little consistency between employers about what they call these roles") — choose by the work described, not the title's prestige. - DA — "the job is analysing and building dashboards." Most of the time goes *before* the analysis: cleaning and validating data, fighting over which definition of a metric is right, clarifying what the request even asks — and a share of finished dashboards are never used at all. It is partly a customer-service job (practitioner essays, Towards Data Science / Data With Sarah [community]; corroborated by the Anaconda time split). - DS — "the job is building models." All model work combined is ~26% of the week (Anaconda 2022); the rest is cleaning, ad-hoc requests ("pull this number for tomorrow's meeting"), and selling results to decision-makers who are often not data-literate (Anaconda 2021: only 36% of respondents called their decision-makers "very data literate"). - MLE — "it's data science with more models." nodes.label: 6. Chart form (Q5) [Recommendation]
nodes.text: 6. Chart form (Q5) [Recommendation] Primary form: grouped horizontal bars — one group per skill (8 groups), four bars per group (DA, DE, DS, MLE in a fixed order and fixed colours), all on the shared 1–5 scale, with the number printed at the end of each bar. The page's primary reading task is per-skill comparison across roles ("which role needs the most SQL?"), which is exactly the task radar performs worst at in every empirical test found and bars perform best at (Cleveland & McGill's perceptual hierarchy: position on a common scale is judged most accurately; angle and area — radar's encodings — least). Acceptable alternative: small multiples — four panels, one per role, each showing that role's eight skills as bars on the identical scale — if the design wants per-role profiles. If a radar is kept anyway (secondary/decorative only), the conditions from the sources: never overlay all four roles (one role per chart, at most two overlaid); one fixed axis order everywhere; identical 1–5 scale with labelled gridlines; no area fill, or only a very light one; print the numbers beside it; and never invite "bigger shape = better role" readings in the text — the shape is partly an artefact of axis order (§1, finding 10). One design note: our lessons are static pages with no JavaScript in lessons. A bar chart is a static image or pure CSS; nothing in this recommendation requires interactivity. ---

nodes.text: 7. Open questions for the design brainstorm 1. DS communication: 4 (frameworks) or 3 (postings)? The frameworks describe the job's output, the ads its inputs. If the page's promise is "what the job is really like," 4 stands; if "what gets you hired," 3 is defensible. The table takes 4, Medium confidence. 2. Does the Experiments axis earn its place at Low confidence, or should it fold into Statistics with a note that A/B testing is a DS specialism? Keeping it is this package's recommendation — but it is the one axis whose scores a single new evidence source could move. 3. When does the ML axis split? LLM/GenAI work (RAG, agents, LLM frameworks) already appears inside MLE and DS postings. A future "GenAI and LLM systems" axis would change MLE's shape most; the split trigger needs a rule (e.g. appears in a majority of MLE postings in a re-sample). 4. Re-sample cadence. The posting sample is dated 2026-11-19 and entry-level MLE evidence is the thinnest. A yearly re-sample of the same boards/countries would keep the page honest; the MLE column should be revisited first. 5. Retire the blanket "math-heavy" line? §4 recommends per-track messages instead. That changes track-page copy beyond this page — owner call. ---

nodes.label: 1. The 10 most useful findings
nodes.text: 1. The 10 most useful findings 1. The capability story is a collapse curve, and one paper draws it. The Spider 2.0 paper (ICLR 2025) measures the same o1-preview code agent at 91.2% success on Spider 1.0 (tidy schemas), 73.0% on BIRD (large, noisy databases), and 21.3% on Spider 2.0's enterprise workflows (schemas of 1,000+ columns, multiple dialects, multi-step deliverables). Nothing about the model changed — the *realism* did. This single comparison is the most teachable capability fact we have. 2. Multi-step work is where AI is worst — and where it is improving fastest. DABstep (June 2025): the best agent scored 14.55% on Hard multi-step analysis tasks (Easy split up to 80.56%). A 2026 preprint tabulating later leaderboard results reports Hard-split scores of 48.68–69.58% — a several-fold rise in about a year. METR's cross-year measurement explains the tempo: frontier models' 50%-completion time horizon has been "doubling approximately every seven months since 2019" (arXiv:2503.14499). Any capability number printed in a lesson needs an "as of" date; the *checks* do not expire. 3. Statistics fails at method choice, not arithmetic. On StatQA (NeurIPS 2024; 11,623 examples), the best model (GPT-4o) reached 64.83%, and the paper's key finding is the error *type*: LLMs primarily make applicability errors — applying a test whose assumptions the data does not meet — whereas humans mostly make task-confusion errors. The AI failure a learner must catch is a confidently wrong *choi…

nodes.label: 4. Fundamentals as detectors (Q3)
nodes.text: 4. Fundamentals as detectors (Q3) The over-reliance evidence (Cluster Q comment, Part B) in one paragraph: explanations do not reduce over-reliance — cognitive forcing functions do (Buçinca et al. 2021, pre-2024); participants with an AI assistant wrote *less* secure code while believing it *more* secure (Perry et al., CCS 2023); automation bias is measured across 74 studies in clinical decision support (Goddard et al. 2012, pre-2024) and a 2025 review finds explanations "may inadvertently reinforce misplaced trust, especially among less experienced professionals with low AI literacy" (Romeo & Conti 2025). nodes.label: 7. Planted-error exercises on the café dataset [Recommendation]
nodes.text: 7. Planted-error exercises on the café dataset [Recommendation] Each drill: the learner receives an AI-produced artefact (query, script or short analysis) containing one planted failure from §3, on the small café sales dataset whose correct answers are known. Flagged version first (the error class is named), unflagged later. Every drill ends with the learner naming the check, not just the error. 1. The doubled revenue. A SQL query joins orders to order_items, then sums `orders.total` — revenue comes out roughly double. (Failure 2: fan-out.) Check: row counts before/after the join; state the grain. 2. The function that isn't. A pandas script calls a plausible, non-existent method to compute daily totals. (Failure 1.) Check: find it in the installed version's docs — it isn't there. 3. The vanishing unhappy customers. A filter `WHERE rating <> 'bad'` silently drops every NULL-rated order from a satisfaction analysis; the reported average quietly improves. (Failure 3.) Check: NULL profile; `COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(rating)`. 4. The average of averages. The AI averages the seven daily average-basket values to get the weekly figure. (Failures 2/4: wrong grain.) Check: recompute from raw rows; the two numbers disagree. 5. The helpful p-hacker. Given café sales and asked to "find what the new promotion changed," the AI tries a dozen cuts and reports the one significant result, triumphantly. (Failure 4.) Check: how many tests were run? nodes.label: Working with AI in data work — what AI can and cannot do, and the human knowledge that catches its mistakes
nodes.text: Working with AI in data work — what AI can and cannot do, and the human knowledge that catches its mistakes What this is. The last part of the advanced core — the part learners finish just before choosing a track — teaches working with AI: prompting with the data in the room, verifying AI output, and judging RAG and agents. This package strengthens that part with primary-source evidence only: benchmark papers and leaderboards (with snapshot dates), peer-reviewed studies, official reports (WEF, McKinsey, LinkedIn/Microsoft, OECD, UNESCO, NIST), and official course pages. Every figure is quoted exactly as its source states it; pre-2024 sources are flagged. Full working files are posted as comments on this issue (Clusters P, Q, R). The one-sentence version. Current AI is a strong drafter and a weak authority: on tidy, well-specified tasks it performs near the ceiling of old benchmarks, and on realistic data work — big undocumented schemas, multi-step workflows, method choice, facts from memory — measured success falls to between roughly one task in five and two in three, with failures that run cleanly and look plausible. The skills that catch those failures are the fundamentals this roadmap already teaches. That is the part's thesis, and every section below is evidence for it. ---

nodes.label: 1. The 10 most useful findings
nodes.text: 1. The 10 most useful findings 1. Data modeling is the strongest topic in the package — stronger than the team expected. 8 of 9 junior-DE postings in the named sample name it; the UK DDaT framework sets Data modelling at Working for the entry DE grade ("produce, maintain and update relevant data models… reverse-engineer data models from a live system"); and Meta's official onsite guide builds an entire interview round around it ("design a data mart… dimensional modeling… denormalization"). It is the only one of the seven topics with a named big-tech interview round. The team's "maybe core" is confirmed and upgraded: core, at use depth. 2. The team's second expectation — "internals (4, 5, 6) belong to the DE track" — is refuted as stated, and refined. For each of topics 4, 5 and 6 the evidence supports a two-layer placement: recognize-level concepts in the core (extending lessons the SQL stage already has — one indexes/plans lesson, one scale lesson), and use/explain depth in the DE track. What is DE-only is the *depth*, not the topic. A learner who will never open the DE track still meets slow queries, mid-refresh number changes, and warehouse vocabulary in every role. 3. Relational algebra/calculus is the package's clearest skip. Zero mentions in every posting, framework, interview guide and practitioner curriculum opened (19 postings; Meta's two official guides; DataLemur's DE guide; DDaT; the Zoomcamp; Dataquest's 30-course DE path). nodes.label: 5. The DE-track "database internals" module [Recommendation]
nodes.text: 5. The DE-track "database internals" module [Recommendation] Eleven lessons, in order. Everything runs free: PostgreSQL in Docker (or a browser Postgres), DuckDB, SQLite — the tools the roadmap already uses. No CS degree assumed: each lesson starts from a café-scale table and a question, and the internals arrive as the answer. nodes.label: 6. Trap bank — the misconceptions worth turning into exercises
nodes.text: 6. Trap bank — the misconceptions worth turning into exercises One flagship trap per topic (Cluster N's comment holds the full bank of 26, each marked demonstrable or not). Every trap below is Demo: YES unless noted — the learner watches the belief break in a real run. 1. Modeling — "If I join the tables I need, the numbers will be right." Joining at the wrong grain multiplies rows: sum `orders.total` before vs after joining order_items in DuckDB; the row counts around the join expose the fan-out. The single most valuable modeling exercise in the bank. 2. Procedures/triggers — "A trigger fires once per statement." In PostgreSQL a row-level trigger fires once per affected *row*, and a statement-level trigger fires even when zero rows are affected. One UPDATE, five audit rows; a second UPDATE matching nothing, one statement-level firing. 3. Algebra — "SQL runs in the order it is written." The alias-in-WHERE error (logical order is FROM → WHERE → … → SELECT), then the same query's EXPLAIN tree read bottom-up. Its twin: "reordering joins changes the answer" — for inner joins it changes cost, never the result; two join orders, identical results, different plans. 4. Indexing — "An index always speeds up a query." On a small table the planner ignores the index on purpose; forcing it costs more. Companion: `WHERE lower(name) = …` cannot use a plain index on `name` — Seq Scan until an expression index exists. 5. Concurrency — "Transactions make concurrent updates safe at any isolatio…

nodes.label: Database internals beyond the SQL stage — how deep, for whom, and where each topic belongs
nodes.text: Database internals beyond the SQL stage — how deep, for whom, and where each topic belongs What this is. The SQL stage (spine: Northeastern CS 5200, issue #52) teaches databases at use depth: querying, keys and grain, joins, aggregation, window functions, CTEs, views, CREATE TABLE and constraints, DML in transactions, one normalization lesson, one indexes-and-query-plans lesson, and one "beyond one database" lesson. A full DBMS course covers seven more topics that stage teaches lightly or not at all: (1) domain/conceptual modeling, (2) stored procedures and triggers, (3) relational algebra and calculus, (4) storage, query processing and indexing, (5) concurrency, transactions and recovery, (6) database architectures, (7) data warehousing, OLAP and data mining. This package answers, from primary sources only: how deep each topic must go per role, where each belongs (core / DE track / DS track / skip), what a DE-track internals module should contain, and which misconceptions are worth turning into exercises. Every cell of the depth table carries its primary sources; all sources were accessed 2026-11-19. Full working files are posted as comments on this issue (Clusters M, N, O). Depth scale. — = no evidence of need · R = recognize (know what it is, read about it, answer concept questions) · U = use (do it in the job with real tools) · E = explain internals (how it works inside, and why) · B = build (implement it — appears only in CMU 15-445, and in no job source). ---

nodes.label: AI-era design rules (each tied to its source)
nodes.text: AI-era design rules (each tied to its source) 1. Print the AI rules on the brief: this is a Full-AI task (AIAS Level 4); the documentation is graded. (Perkins et al. 2024; Berkeley CTL on stating permitted levels.) 2. Decisive context lives only in the brief — the budget, the decision-maker, the constraint — nowhere public; generic advice that ignores it is visibly wrong. (Western CTL: GenAI is "not able to draw on the specifics of these examples in their responses"; Berkeley CTL on course-specific relevance.) 3. The dataset carries unannounced quirks visible only by running it (here: the duplicate structure, the pre-1910 births, the missing household ID); finding them is the cleaning grade. Prefer real quirks; plant at most one, disclosed in teacher notes. [Recommendation] (DABstep/Spider 2.0 failure evidence.) 4. Verification log: one row per AI output — output, check performed, accept / revise / reject + reason. (OECD/EC Engage 3, Advanced: "Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them"; Bearman et al. 2024, focus 1.) 5. The rubric grades the chain, not the answer — several defensible decisions score full marks. (Western CTL: "nuanced real-world examples without a single correct answer"; Berkeley CTL: assess "how they got there"; TEQSA: assess "the process of learning.") 6. Explain-back in the learner's own words: method, why, and the one number they would defend. (Bearman et al. 2024, focus 2 — judging AI *processes*.) 7. Cl…

nodes.label: Key findings
nodes.text: Key findings 1. No top-university case is both free and freely reusable in full. The strongest university cases sit under NonCommercial and/or ShareAlike licenses (MIT OCW and CMU OLI: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; Berkeley textbooks: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; Berkeley course materials: CC BY-NC 4.0) or behind a paywall (Harvard Business School). The lawful pattern for every university winner is the same: link to their case, host nothing of theirs, write our own brief — and let learners download the data from the source. 2. MIT OCW's license, verbatim, bars the obvious route. OCW's terms name "Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)" and MIT adds that users "may not sell, profit from, or commercialize OCW materials or works derived from them." Under CC's own ShareAlike rule, an adaptation's license "must be a Creative Commons license with the same License Elements" — so OCW text or data can never be republished inside our CC BY 4.0 pages. 3. HBS cases are excluded, on HBP's own words. Cases are sold per copy (a current case lists at $11.95 with "purchase one copy per user" copyright permission), HBP's terms claim the contents as "the sole property of HBP or its licensors" with no copying or derivatives without written permission, and its permissions page states "we do not grant permission for any adaptation, edit, excerpt or summary of any case." Baker Library confirms active cases go only to enrolled HBS students; everyone else must purchase. 4. The strongest cas…

nodes.label: Licensing verdicts — what a CC BY 4.0 site may do
nodes.text: Licensing verdicts — what a CC BY 4.0 site may do - MIT OCW candidates (1, 5, 6): link only + write our own brief. Linking triggers neither the NC term nor ShareAlike. Adapting OCW text, or hosting its CSVs, would force CC BY-NC-SA on the result — incompatible with our CC BY 4.0 pages. Learners download data from OCW. MIT's name may be credited, not used as branding. - LEGO (2): adapt the article's text with attribution (CC BY 4.0); link for the data. The dataset is the article's supplement with no license line of its own; host nothing unless the authors confirm. - Berkeley CCAO (3): link to Berkeley's case study; build our brief on the county's data once the Cook County portal's license is verified. Berkeley's own text: link only (textbook CC BY-NC-ND; notes state no license). - OpenIntro (4): link only. Text is CC BY-SA 3.0 (an adaptation must stay BY-SA 3.0) and the data package is GPL-3; neither folds into CC BY 4.0 pages. - FiveThirtyEight (7): link, adapt, and host the data with attribution (CC BY 4.0) — the only candidate with an unambiguous hostable data license; it is not a university case and its data are from 2010–2012. - Open Case Studies (9): link only (CC BY-NC cannot be republished as CC BY). Open Policing (10): the data is reusable under ODC-By with attribution, but its scale (the site itself warns datasets are "too large for Excel") and sensitive domain rule it out here. - General rules (from CC's own texts): CC0 and US federal public-domain material may be…

nodes.label: Research: a real, openly licensed case study for the advanced-core capstone
nodes.text: Research: a real, openly licensed case study for the advanced-core capstone Question. Find ONE real case study from a top university — free to the public and legally reusable — to serve as the capstone after the advanced core: solvable in Excel, SQL or Python, domain-neutral, with an open answer (several defensible decisions, graded on reasoning), and designed for the AI era (learners will use AI; the case and its reference answer are built for that). Method. Five evidence clusters, all primary sources, accessed 2026-11-20, license lines quoted verbatim: MIT + Harvard; Stanford + Berkeley + CMU; open case collections; licensing compatibility + alternative datasets; AI-era assessment design. The top candidate was also tested live: its data file was downloaded, a ground-truth analysis computed independently, and the capstone question put to a current AI assistant (Muse Spark, 2026-11-20) whose answer was graded number by number. Detail in the evidence comments on this issue.

nodes.label: The capstone, sketched for #1
nodes.text: The capstone, sketched for #1 The case (our own brief, linking OCW's assignment and data). *The 40,000-letter decision.* "A civic-engagement campaign is preparing for a low-turnout primary. In 2006, researchers randomly assigned ~344,000 Michigan voters to no letter or one of four mailings of escalating social pressure (Civic Duty; Hawthorne; Self; Neighbors — descriptions in the linked source). The campaign can afford at most 40,000 letters. Decide: which mailing, if any, should it send — and should it target particular voters rather than mail at random? Defend the decision with numbers and uncertainty, state what would change your mind, and keep a verification log of every AI output you used." Why the answer is open. The most effective mailing (Neighbors, +8.1 pp) is also the one that shows people their neighbors' records — a campaign may defensibly reject it on ethics/reputation grounds and choose Self (+4.9 pp) or a targeted Neighbors mailing; a campaign may also defensibly argue the 2006 primary does not transfer to its election and propose a pilot instead. All can earn full marks; a bare "send Neighbors, it has the biggest number" cannot. Deliverables. (1) A cleaned analysis table (one row per voter, group as one column — the modeling step) with a short data-quality note; (2) one model or schema (e.g. a logistic model or a group×segment effect table) with a one-line justification; (3) 3–5 key numbers with intervals (turnout by group; each mailing's effect vs control; e…

nodes.label: The live AI test, and the draft reference-answer section
nodes.text: The live AI test, and the draft reference-answer section Test protocol (2026-11-20). The capstone question above was given, with the actual `gerber.csv`, to a current general-purpose AI assistant (Muse Spark) with code execution, in a fresh session with no hints about traps. Its full answer is preserved in the evidence for this package. What it got right. Every headline number matched the independently computed ground truth: baseline 29.7%; effects +1.8 / +2.6 / +4.9 / +8.1 pp with intervals matching to rounding; ≈3,250 extra votes per 40,000 Neighbors letters; no sex targeting (+8.2 vs +8.1 pp); the age pattern (twenties +3.7 pp; 60–69 +10.8 pp; targeting 30–69 ≈ 3,500 per 40,000, "about 81%" of the electorate — verified 81.1%). It flagged the ethics of the Neighbors letter, the one-election limit, and the uncheckable clustering. It invented no variables and no sources — it correctly noted that past voting history, the usual targeting variable, is *not* in the file. What it skipped or got subtly wrong. (1) It never mentioned the duplicate structure — it neither fell for it nor explained it, so a learner who asks a follow-up ("should I drop duplicates?") is unprotected. (2) It fitted no model and produced no schema — raw differences only (defensible for a randomized experiment, short of the capstone's deliverable). (3) It ran no reported data-quality checks (no missingness, exclusivity, or yob-plausibility check). (4) Its headline recommendation — "target ages 30–69" — rests…

nodes.label: Top 3 [Recommendation]
nodes.text: Top 3 [Recommendation] 1. [Recommendation] MIT 15.071, "Understanding Why People Vote" — the best case on pedagogy, decision quality and checkability; used via link + our own brief (§5 sketch). Its license is the constraint, not a defect: our brief, rubric and reference answer are entirely ours. 2. [Recommendation] JSDSE LEGO pricing case — the only candidate whose text we may adapt (CC BY 4.0), a published article to check against, and a clean small dataset; the fallback if the team wants adaptable source text. Data still link-only. 3. [Recommendation] Berkeley Data 100 Cook County case — the richest real-world decision and the only candidate whose data comes from an open government program (so a fully ours, hostable capstone is plausible) — conditional on verifying the Cook County data license before building.

nodes.label: Principles (in priority order)
nodes.text: Principles (in priority order) 1. Permanence. Every published URL keeps working forever. Content outlives the framework. 2. Stability & speed. Static site, minimal JavaScript, works with JS disabled, fast on a phone. 3. Academic quality. Versioned, citable (DOI), sourced, dated, reviewed. 4. Beginner-first. Audience knows only Microsoft Office; most read on phones. 5. Delight, sparingly. GSAP motion only on the homepage (D28). ---

nodes.label: Design & motion
nodes.text: Design & motion - Tokens, typography and logo rules: see `design/README.md` §2–3. Dark is default; every page, the homepage included, has a light theme behind the switch in the bottom taskbar (D9, D31); `@media print` forces black-on-white, hides nav/buttons, prints link URLs. - Every page has the bottom taskbar (D31, D35: on phones it is the only navigation). Off the homepage it is the only script beyond Starlight's own (under 1 KB gzipped, CSS transitions only), except the career quiz's one scoring script on `/career-quiz/` (D33: under 4 KB gzipped, no GSAP, no storage). - GSAP is allowed on the homepage `/` only, any plugin, each effect loaded on demand (D28). Project pages (`/start/`, `/about/`, `/cite/`, `/changelog/`, `/license/`, `/privacy/`), stories, lessons, reference and datasets load no motion script. - Every animation respects `prefers-reduced-motion`; all content is visible with JS disabled. - Page-to-page navigation uses CSS-only cross-document View Transitions (D26) and Speculation Rules prefetch (D27); neither adds executable JS to lesson pages. - Study pages (lessons): wide line-height, max ~70ch, one idea per section. Reference pages: compact, scannable, fixed section order (§5.2). ---

nodes.label: Analytics & privacy
nodes.text: Analytics & privacy - Google Analytics 4, loaded only after consent (Consent Mode v2, default `denied`). - A consent card laid out like the owner's johnha.info (owner decision, 2026-11-17): a glass card floating at the bottom (centered on phones, bottom-left of the content on wide screens), always above the bottom taskbar and hidden while the taskbar menu is open. Reject all and Accept all have equal weight; Customize opens "Strictly necessary" (always on) and an Analytics switch with Save choices. Choice remembered; "Cookie settings" link in the footer to change it. - Declining must leave the site fully functional; GA script must never block rendering. - The Measurement ID is the single value `GA_ID` in `src/site.ts`. While it is empty there is no banner, no GA code, no "Cookie settings" link and no added JavaScript. The choice is kept in `localStorage` key `dfz-consent`; only page views are collected for now. - `/privacy/` page states what is collected, why, retention, and how to opt out. - Events worth tracking (optional): `open_in_colab`, `open_in_sheets`, `show_solution`, `report_issue`. > Note: GA plus a banner costs some speed and simplicity; it was chosen for richer insight. > If the banner hurts the experience, GoatCounter (no cookies, no banner) is the drop-in fallback. ---

nodes.label: Quality gates (CI on every PR and on `main`)
nodes.text: Quality gates (CI on every PR and on `main`) | Check | Tool | Blocks merge | |---|---|---| | Build + schema validation | `astro build` (Zod content collections) | Yes | | Internal links & anchors | `starlight-links-validator` | Yes | | Prerequisite / see-also ids exist; no cycles in prerequisites; `order` follows prerequisites within a stage (D25) | `scripts/check-graph.ts` | Yes | | External links | `lychee` (weekly scheduled job, opens an issue) | No | | Spelling (American English) | `cspell` with project dictionary | Yes | | Markdown style | `markdownlint` | Yes | | Notebooks have no outputs | `nbstripout --verify` | Yes | | Accessibility + performance | Lighthouse CI on `/`, one lesson, one reference page | Yes if a budget is missed | Budgets: Lighthouse mobile ≥ 90 (performance), ≥ 95 (accessibility). Lesson pages ship no framework JS beyond Starlight's own and the taskbar script (D31: one script under 1 KB gzipped, no GSAP, no library). JavaScript before first paint ≈ 3 KB gzipped on the homepage; effects load on demand (D28). Motion performance budget: every frame of motion fits 8.3 ms of main-thread work (120 Hz). Per-frame work is O(1) and writes only `transform` and `opacity`; sizes are measured once and on ScrollTrigger's refresh; section setup runs one section per task after a presented frame: sections near the viewport first (also while scrolling, in small slots), the rest after the intro while the reader is idle; a section that fails to build is reverted and the others continue; `will-change` exists only while its animation is active. Measured with `npm run perf` (dev only, noisy, not a CI gate): Chromium, CPU throttled 4×, 390×844 and 1280×800, intro, scroll, warm (the same scroll once every section is built), pointer, history (the homepage slider: buttons, keys, drag), careers (the 05 career figures: each card opened in turn, its canvas loop running) and a docs page. Targets at 4×: no long animation frame above 50 ms after the intro, scroll p95 main-thread frame at or under 16.7 ms (a proxy for 8.3 ms on a real phone), docs pages with zero layout, style and paint work while scrolling. Accessibility target: WCAG 2.2 AA (contrast, keyboard navigation, alt text, MathML). Maintenance: Dependabot monthly, grouped; Node LTS upgraded once a year; Astro/Starlight major upgrades only in their own PR with a full CI pass. `reviewed` dates older than 18 months are listed by a scheduled job. ---

nodes.label: Content production (replaces migration, D24)
nodes.text: Content production (replaces migration, D24) Content is written from scratch; `johnha912/data-odyssey` is not migrated. 1. Curriculum map. Research proposes every lesson per stage (id, slug, title, order, level, duration, objectives, prerequisites, key sources). The owner approves the map once; slugs then become permanent (§3). 2. Stubs. Approved lessons are created as `status: draft` files (never deployed, D18). The build validates ids, prerequisites and cycles from day one. 3. Writing. The owner writes the lesson text, or asks the team for a draft text that the owner edits and approves (D24). The team adds or completes frontmatter, exercises and solutions, notebooks, Google Sheets templates, datasets (§7), `Term` links and sources, and keeps the build green. 4. Publishing. The owner reviews and sets `status: published`. Vietnamese translations follow in later PRs (§8). 5. Release. Tag `v1.0.0` once the four core stages are published; enable Zenodo; publish `CITATION.cff` (§9). Counts (D49): 195 lessons in 8 stages; the advanced core is 43 lessons in six parts plus a capstone of about four hours, one project growing part by part. The DSA practice gym is planned after the tracks exist; nothing is built.

nodes.label: Explicitly out of scope (for now)
nodes.text: Explicitly out of scope (for now) Accounts, saved progress, comments, in-browser code execution (except the SQL runner of D42: DuckDB-Wasm, self-hosted, loaded in the background near a block, no storage), paid content, newsletters, AI chat on the site. Each would need a new decision entry in §1 before being built.
